lessons.title: Coaptation, long-arm and finger splints: the build, step by step
lessons.body:
## The coaptation splint

A broken humeral shaft is not held rigid. It is hung. The splint is a long U of plaster or prepadded fiberglass that starts high in the armpit, runs down the inside of the arm, turns around the elbow, and comes back up the outside of the arm and over the top of the shoulder. Gravity pulls the arm down inside that U and pulls the fracture ends into line.

1. Measure on the uninjured arm: armpit, around the elbow held at `90 degrees`, up over the deltoid. In an adult that is usually `75-100 cm`.
2. Stockinette and padding first, with an extra layer in the armpit and over the bony point of the elbow (olecranon).
3. Lay the slab so the outer limb ends **on top of** the shoulder, not below it. A short outer limb slides off and the whole splint rotates.
4. Wrap with an elastic bandage from the elbow upward, then take a second wrap around the chest to anchor the top.
5. Sling and swathe go on last. The sling carries the forearm, the swathe stops the arm swinging.

This is a two-person build. One holds, one wraps.

> **Trap:** A coaptation splint that stops below the shoulder does nothing at all. The outer limb has to come over the deltoid so the wrap has something to grip.

## Posterior long-arm, with and without side struts

The standard posterior long-arm is a slab from the back of the upper arm, around the elbow at `90 degrees`, out along the little-finger side of the forearm, ending at the wrist crease or the knuckles depending on what has to be held. Forearm neutral, thumb pointing at the ceiling.

Add **side struts** (a double sugar-tong: radial and ulnar strips laid alongside the posterior slab) when the elbow or proximal forearm is unstable and blocking bending is not enough. The struts block rotation as well. They are bulkier and heavier, so they are not the default.

## Gutter splints, built

**Ulnar gutter.** A slab long enough to run from the fingertips of the ring and little fingers, along the little-finger side of the hand and forearm, stopping about `2-3 cm` short of the elbow crease. Fold it lengthwise into a shallow trough. Put padding **between** the ring and little fingers before it goes on, or two skin surfaces sit wet against each other and break down. Wrist extended about `20 degrees`, knuckles (MCPs) bent `70-90 degrees`, finger joints nearly straight.

**Radial gutter.** The mirror image on the thumb side for the index and middle fingers, with a hole cut in the slab for the thumb before it is applied.

## Thumb spica variations

- **Short-arm (wrist-based) thumb spica:** stops below the elbow. Fits de Quervain tenosynovitis and stable thumb metacarpal injuries.
- **Long-arm thumb spica:** crosses the elbow. Chosen when rotation has to be blocked, as in a proximal scaphoid fracture.
- **How far out the thumb goes** depends on the injury. A ulnar collateral ligament tear (skier's thumb) needs the thumb MCP joint held; many scaphoid splints stop at the thumb interphalangeal joint and leave the tip free.

## Finger splints by injury

| Injury | Splint | Position |
|---|---|---|
| Mallet finger | Stack or foam splint on the DIP only | DIP straight or slightly hyperextended, continuous `6-8 weeks`, PIP left free |
| Central slip injury (boutonniere) | Splint across the PIP | PIP straight, DIP free to move |
| Volar plate injury, PIP hyperextension sprain | Dorsal extension-block splint | PIP blocked at `20-30 degrees` of flexion |
| Stable non-displaced phalanx fracture | Buddy tape | Gauze between the fingers, tape above and below the joint |
| Tuft fracture after nail bed repair | Aluminum-foam fingertip splint | Protects the repair, tip visible |

> **Key:** Mallet finger is the one splint that never comes off, not even to wash. Let the fingertip droop once and the clock starts over.

## Fitting what comes prefabricated

A **knee immobilizer** that slides down the leg is the wrong length, not the wrong tightness. A **CAM boot** is fitted with the heel seated all the way back, straps tightened from the ankle outward, and the patient needs a lift on the other shoe or they walk crooked for weeks. A **stirrup ankle brace** goes on over a sock, never bare skin, and the air cells are inflated after the straps are set.

> **On shift:** Whatever you build, show the patient the fingers or toes you deliberately left exposed. They are the ones who will notice the color change at two in the morning.
keyPoints: Coaptation runs armpit, around the elbow, over the deltoid, and always gets a sling and swathe.
Side struts turn a posterior long-arm into a rotation-blocking splint for an unstable elbow or proximal forearm.
Ulnar gutter: padding between the ring and little fingers, MCPs 70-90 degrees, finger joints nearly straight.
Mallet finger is splinted at the DIP in full extension, continuously, for 6-8 weeks, with the PIP free.
A volar plate injury gets a dorsal extension-block splint at 20-30 degrees, not a straight splint.

checks.q: A coaptation splint keeps sliding down and rotating off a patient's arm. What is the most likely build error?
choices: The outer limb of the U stopped below the shoulder instead of crossing the deltoid
Too many layers of plaster were used
The elbow was held at 90 degrees
The padding was rolled distal to proximal
checks.why: The elastic wrap needs the shoulder to grip against. An outer limb that stops on the upper arm has nothing holding it, so the splint migrates. Layer count, elbow angle and padding direction are all correct as described.

checks.q: A 24-year-old jammed her ring finger on a basketball and now cannot straighten the fingertip. How is this splinted?
choices: Buddy tape to the little finger for 7 days
DIP joint held straight continuously for 6-8 weeks, with the PIP left free
Ulnar gutter with the MCPs at 70-90 degrees
Dorsal extension block at 20-30 degrees
checks.why: This is a mallet finger: the extensor tendon is off the distal phalanx. Only continuous DIP extension lets it heal, and the PIP must stay free to avoid stiffness. Buddy tape does not hold extension, a gutter treats metacarpal injuries, and extension block treats volar plate injuries.

checks.q: What goes between the ring and little fingers before an ulnar gutter splint is applied?
choices: Nothing; skin contact keeps the fingers aligned
A layer of padding, so two skin surfaces do not macerate against each other
A tongue depressor to hold them straight
A thin coat of tissue adhesive
checks.why: Skin held against skin under a splint stays damp and breaks down within a day or two. Padding separates them. A rigid depressor would fight the 70-90 degree MCP position, and adhesive has no role inside a splint.

lessons.title: Casting and cast removal with the saw
lessons.body:
## Why a cast instead of a splint

A splint is rigid on one or two sides so a swelling limb has somewhere to expand. A cast is rigid all the way around, which holds a fracture better and defeats a patient who will not stay still. The trade is that a cast on a limb that is still swelling squeezes, and squeezed muscle inside its tough sheath is compartment syndrome.

So the usual sequence is splint in the emergency department, cast at orthopedic follow-up in `3-7 days`, once swelling has peaked and started down. Casts do get applied in the department, usually by orthopedics, for a stable fracture in a limb that is already several days out from the injury.

## The build

The layers are the same as a splint. The difference is that the material goes all the way around.

1. Stockinette, wrinkle-free, cut `10 cm` longer than the cast at each end.
2. Cast padding rolled distal to proximal, each turn covering half of the last, `2-3 layers`, extra over bony points, `2` extra turns at each end. Padding that bunches becomes a pressure sore in a day.
3. Roll the plaster or fiberglass on **without tension**. You unroll it and let it lie down on the limb. Pulling the roll tight is how a cast becomes a tourniquet.
4. Laminate each turn into the last with flat wet palms.
5. Fold the stockinette and padding back over both ends and secure with a final turn.
6. Mold with palms, never fingertips, and hold the joint position until firm: plaster `10-15 minutes`, fiberglass `3-5 minutes`.

A wet cast is not a strong cast. Plaster needs `24-48 hours` before weight bearing. Fiberglass is near full strength in about `30 minutes`.

> **Trap:** Rolling cast material under tension feels like careful technique and is the most common reason a cast has to be cut off the same night.

## What goes wrong

- **Too tight:** pain, numbness, swelling, pale or cold digits, and pain when the fingers or toes are gently straightened.
- **Pressure sore:** a burning hot spot the patient can point to, sometimes with drainage or a smell days later.
- **Skin injury from something pushed inside** to scratch an itch.
- **Wet cast:** softens, loses its shape, and macerates the skin underneath.
- **Thermal injury:** hot dip water plus a thick cast plus a blanket laid over it while it cures.

There is no telephone fix for any of those. A patient who calls with them comes back in.

## Univalve, bivalve, and windows

When a cast is tight but does not have to come off entirely, the options escalate:

- **Univalve:** cut one side of the cast and spread it. That alone drops the pressure inside meaningfully.
- **Bivalve:** cut both sides so the cast becomes two shells held together by the elastic wrap. This relieves the most pressure and is what happens on the way to the operating room.
- **Window:** a square cut out over a wound so it can be inspected, then taped back in place so the skin does not swell up into the hole.

The padding has to be cut as well. A cast split with the cotton still intact underneath relieves very little, and that is the classic incomplete job.

## The saw

The blade does not spin. It oscillates through a tiny arc at roughly `15,000-20,000` cycles per minute. Rigid cast material cannot move with it, so it is cut. Skin is soft, moves with the blade, and is skidded over instead.

That is only true if the technique is right.

- Cut **in and out**, lifting and repositioning the blade, never dragging it along like a knife.
- Cut along the flat sides of the limb and **stay off bony prominences**, where the padding is thinnest.
- Feel the blade. Hot or dull burns. Change it.
- Never saw over skin on a patient who cannot feel or cannot report. A sedated, confused, or neuropathic patient is the classic saw burn.
- Spread with the cast spreader, then cut the padding with bandage scissors, blunt tip against the skin.

Tell the patient first: it is loud, it gets warm, it does not cut skin, and they should speak the instant anything feels sharp or hot.

> **On shift:** Eye protection and a mask for you, and a towel over the patient's face if they want one. Cast dust gets into everything.
keyPoints: A cast is circumferential, so it holds better and squeezes harder; the ED usually splints first and casts at follow-up in 3-7 days.
Cast material is unrolled without tension; pulling it tight is the classic cause of a cast that must be cut off.
Univalve relieves pressure, bivalve relieves more, and the padding must be cut too or little changes.
The cast saw oscillates rather than spins: cut in and out, avoid bony prominences, change a hot or dull blade.
Plaster needs 24-48 hours before weight bearing; fiberglass is near full strength in about 30 minutes.

checks.q: Why does a cast saw blade usually not cut skin?
choices: The blade is coated with a skin-safe polymer
The blade oscillates through a small arc, so soft skin moves with it instead of being cut
The blade spins slowly enough that skin is not damaged
A plastic guard keeps the blade off the skin
checks.why: Oscillation is the whole mechanism: rigid material cannot move with the blade and is cut, while skin deflects. The blade is not coated, does not spin, and has no guard, which is why bad technique still burns people.

checks.q: A tight cast is bivalved, but the patient's pain and numbness do not improve. What was most likely missed?
choices: The cast should have been windowed instead
The padding underneath the cast was not cut
The patient needed a second elastic wrap
The cast should have been plaster rather than fiberglass
checks.why: Intact cotton padding is still a circumferential layer and keeps pressure up. Cutting the padding is part of a bivalve. A window inspects a wound rather than relieving pressure, and material choice does not change constriction.

checks.q: Which patient is at the highest risk of a cast saw burn?
choices: An alert 30-year-old having a forearm cast removed
A diabetic patient with neuropathy who cannot feel the blade or report heat
A child who is crying during the removal
A patient in fiberglass rather than plaster
checks.why: The patient's own report is the main safety net. Someone who cannot feel the blade never warns you, so the burn is discovered afterward. A crying but sensate child will react, and material type does not determine burn risk.

lessons.title: Inside the suture tray: instruments, needles and assisting the repair
lessons.body:
## The instruments, and what each one is for

- **Needle driver (needle holder):** short, blunt, box-locked jaws that grip the needle. The needle is loaded about one third of the way back from the swage and at a right angle to the jaws.
- **Adson forceps with teeth:** the small tissue forceps with two tiny prongs meeting one. Teeth grip skin with less crushing than flat smooth jaws, which have to squeeze harder to hold. Smooth forceps are for suture, gauze and dressings, not skin.
- **Iris or suture scissors:** fine and sharp, for cutting thread only. Cutting wire or staples with them ruins them.
- **Skin hooks:** lift a wound edge with no crush at all. They are sharp, so they are passed tip-down.
- **Hemostats:** clamp a bleeder, hold a packing strip, break up the pockets inside an abscess.
- **Scalpel:** an `11` blade to stab and drain, a `15` blade for a fine curved cut, a `10` blade for a longer incision.

On the field: fenestrated drape, `4x4` gauze, the suture the provider asked for, a `10 mL` syringe with a `25-27 gauge` needle, saline in a basin. A sharps container within the provider's arm reach, not across the room.

## Needles: point, curve and size

Suture packets read like a code, and one distinction decides most of it.

- **Cutting** needles have a triangular cross-section with the sharp edge on the **inside** of the curve. They cut tough skin, but the cut runs toward the wound edge.
- **Reverse cutting** needles put the sharp edge on the **outside** of the curve, so the cut runs away from the wound edge and the stitch is less likely to tear out. This is the standard skin needle.
- **Taper** needles are round and pointed with no cutting edge. They spread tissue apart rather than slicing it, which suits bowel, vessel and fascia. They will not pass through skin.
- **Blunt** needles exist to reduce needlestick injuries when suturing fascia.

Curvature is written as a fraction of a circle. `3/8 circle` is the workhorse for skin and `1/2 circle` is for tight spaces where the driver cannot swing.

Skin suture arrives **swaged**: the thread is molded into the back of the needle, so there is no eye and no doubled thread dragging through the tissue. The packet also lists length, commonly `18` or `30 inches`.

> **Trap:** A taper needle handed over for a skin repair will not go through. It is not dull, it is simply the wrong shape for skin.

## Throws, knots and what you actually do

A **throw** is one wrap of thread around the driver and one pull-through. A **knot** is several throws stacked. In an instrument tie, the long end is wrapped around the driver, the short end is grabbed and pulled through, and the throw is laid flat. The direction of the wrap is then **reversed** for the next throw, and that reversal is what makes it a square knot. Wrapping the same direction twice makes a sliding knot that loosens overnight.

Rough throw counts: `3-4` for nylon, `4-5` for polypropylene because it is slippery, `3` for silk. More throws mean a bigger knot sitting under thin skin.

Your job as the assistant is small and specific. Keep the field lit and dry. **Blot** with gauze rather than wiping, because wiping drags clot and tissue off the edges. Hold retraction exactly where asked and do not creep. Cut the suture where and at the length the provider says, usually `5-10 mm` tails on skin. Pass instruments handle-first with the tips controlled, and **announce every sharp out loud, every time it moves.**

## Counts and the record

Count the sharps. Count gauze if the wound is deep enough to hide a sponge. Account for every needle before the drape comes off. Anything removed from the wound goes into a labeled specimen container, because a retained foreign body is a medical and sometimes a legal object.

Document: anesthetic drug, concentration, volume and time; irrigation fluid and volume; suture material and size; number of sutures placed; dressing applied; tetanus given or deferred; the post-repair neurovascular check; and the removal date the patient was told.

> **Key:** Reverse cutting for skin, taper for everything inside. That single distinction explains most of the codes on the suture shelf.

> **On shift:** Ask once how the provider likes the needle loaded, then load it that way every time. It halves the length of the repair.
keyPoints: Toothed Adson forceps hold skin with less crush injury than smooth forceps, which have to squeeze harder.
Reverse cutting needles are the skin standard; taper needles are for tissue inside the body and will not pass skin.
A square knot requires reversing the wrap direction each throw: 3-4 throws for nylon, 4-5 for polypropylene.
The assistant blots rather than wipes, cuts tails at 5-10 mm, and announces every sharp out loud.
Document anesthetic drug and volume, irrigation volume, suture size, number placed, tetanus, dressing and removal date.

checks.q: Which needle type is correct for repairing a skin laceration?
choices: Taper
Reverse cutting
Blunt
Straight taper
checks.why: Reverse cutting puts the sharp edge on the outside of the curve, so the tissue cut runs away from the wound edge and the stitch does not pull through. Taper and blunt needles are for fascia, bowel and vessels and will not penetrate skin cleanly.

checks.q: Why is the wrap direction reversed on each successive throw of an instrument tie?
choices: To use less suture material
To create a square knot rather than a sliding knot that loosens
To reduce the risk of a needlestick
To make the knot easier to find at removal
checks.why: Reversing direction squares the knot so it locks. Wrapping the same way twice produces a slip knot that can loosen after the patient leaves. Suture economy, sharps safety and removal are not affected by throw direction.

checks.q: A provider is repairing a scalp laceration that keeps oozing and asks you to keep the field clear. What is correct?
choices: Wipe the wound with gauze in long strokes
Blot the field with gauze so clot and tissue are not dragged off the edges
Pour hydrogen peroxide in to stop the bleeding
Hold continuous suction against the wound edge
checks.why: Blotting removes fluid without stripping clot or dragging the wound edges out of alignment. Wiping does the opposite, peroxide destroys healing tissue and never goes inside a wound, and continuous suction on the edge causes trauma.

lessons.title: Staples, glue, strips, and the wound that comes apart
lessons.body:
## Staples: placement, and the removal you will do

A skin stapler drives a rectangle of metal that bridges the wound and holds the edges together without anything crossing inside it. That makes it fast, which is why it owns the scalp and long straight wounds on the trunk and limbs. It is not used on the face, on the hands, or where imaging of that exact area is planned soon.

Placing them is usually the provider's job. **Removal** is often yours, and it has a dedicated tool for a reason. The remover has two lower prongs and one upper. Slide the two lower prongs fully under the crossbar of the staple, then squeeze. Squeezing bends the middle of the staple downward, which rotates both legs straight up and out of the skin. Lift gently. Do not drag the staple sideways and do not pry one out with a hemostat.

Timing: scalp `7-10 days`, trunk and limbs `7-14 days`. If any part of the wound looks fragile, remove **every other** staple, lay adhesive strips across, and have the patient rechecked rather than taking them all at once.

> **Trap:** Prying a staple out with a hemostat tears skin and hurts far more than it should. The remover exists because the geometry matters.

## Tissue adhesive, done properly

Skin glue (2-octyl cyanoacrylate) is not a filler. It is a surface bridge, and it only holds if the edges already meet with no tension and no bleeding.

1. Irrigate, then **dry the skin completely**. Glue will not bond to a wet surface.
2. Get hemostasis. A slow ooze lifts the film off from underneath.
3. Hold the edges together, perfectly aligned, with gloved fingers or forceps.
4. Paint the glue **across** the closed wound, extending `5-10 mm` onto the skin on either side. Never let it run down into the wound.
5. Apply `3-4` thin layers, pausing about `30 seconds` between them. Thin stacked layers are stronger than one thick one.
6. Keep holding for about `60 seconds` after the last layer.

For anything on the forehead or brow, position the head so the wound is the highest point and lay a gauze dam along the orbit so nothing runs toward the eye. Glue that reaches the eye is treated with petrolatum ointment and an ophthalmology opinion, never by forcing the lids apart.

No ointment, no soaking, no scrubbing afterward. It sloughs on its own in `5-10 days`, and petroleum jelly or antibiotic ointment dissolves it early.

## Adhesive strips

Thin adhesive strips close a shallow wound with no depth and no tension, and more often they **support** a repair after sutures or staples come out.

Dry the skin, paint **tincture of benzoin** `1-2 cm` to either side and let it get tacky, keeping it out of the wound itself where it stings and inflames. Anchor the first strip on one side, draw the wound edge across, and lay it down on the far side. Leave a gap between strips so fluid can drain, then run one strip parallel on each side crossing all the ends so nothing curls up. They fall off by themselves in `5-10 days`.

## The wound check, and the wound that opens

A recheck at `24-48 hours` is standard for a contaminated wound, a hand wound, a drained abscess, and any diabetic or immunosuppressed patient.

| Finding | What it means |
|---|---|
| Redness `1-2 cm` at the edge, no warmth, pain settling | Normal inflammation |
| Spreading redness, warmth, increasing pain, pus | Infection |
| A red streak tracking up the limb | Lymphangitis; escalate now |
| Edges separated, tissue visible at the base | Dehiscence |
| Dusky skin, crepitus, pain far out of proportion, patient looks sick | Necrotizing infection; this is a resuscitation |

**Dehiscence** is the wound coming apart, from tension, infection, a slipped knot, sutures out too early, steroids, diabetes, or a patient who went back to using the hand. A partly dehisced clean wound is often managed with strips and left to heal from the base up rather than restitched, because sewing old or infected tissue shut traps the problem inside. Your part is to expose it, measure it, document what is visible at the base, and not tape anything closed before a provider has seen it.

> **Key:** Glue and strips fail for the same single reason: tension. A wound under tension gets sutures.

> **On shift:** When a patient comes back with an angry-looking wound, mark the outer edge of the redness with a skin pen and write the time beside it. The next person can then see at a glance whether it is spreading.
keyPoints: The staple remover's two lower prongs go fully under the crossbar; squeezing bends the staple and lifts both legs out.
Scalp staples come out at 7-10 days, trunk and limbs at 7-14; take every other one if the wound looks fragile.
Skin glue goes across a dry, bloodless, tension-free wound in 3-4 thin layers and never into the wound.
Benzoin goes on the skin beside the wound, never in it, and strips are spaced so fluid can drain.
Spreading redness, warmth or pus is infection; a red streak is lymphangitis; pain out of proportion in a sick-looking patient is a surgical emergency.

checks.q: How is a skin staple removed correctly?
choices: Grasp the crossbar with a hemostat and pull straight up
Slide both lower prongs of the remover fully under the crossbar, squeeze, and lift out
Cut the crossbar with suture scissors and pull each leg separately
Rock the staple side to side until it loosens
checks.why: Squeezing the remover bends the staple's midpoint down, which rotates both legs vertically so they lift straight out of their tracks. Pulling, cutting or rocking drags the legs sideways through skin and tears it.

checks.q: A forehead laceration is being closed with tissue adhesive. Which step prevents the most serious complication?
choices: Applying one thick layer so it sets faster
Positioning the head so glue cannot run toward the eye, with a gauze dam along the brow
Applying antibiotic ointment to the skin first
Soaking the area in saline immediately after application
checks.why: Glue running into the eye is the feared complication of forehead and brow repairs, and gravity plus a gauze dam prevents it. One thick layer is weaker than several thin ones, and ointment or soaking dissolves the adhesive.

checks.q: A patient returns three days after a hand laceration repair with a red streak running up the forearm and worsening pain. What does this represent?
choices: Expected healing at day three
Lymphangitis, which needs immediate provider evaluation
An allergic reaction to nylon suture
Dehiscence of the repair
checks.why: A red streak tracking proximally is infection spreading through lymphatic channels and needs antibiotics and reassessment now. Normal healing does not streak, suture allergy is rare and local, and dehiscence means the edges have separated, which is not described.

lessons.title: Procedural sedation support from consent to discharge
lessons.body:
## Sedation is a spectrum, not a switch

| Depth | Patient responds to | Airway | Breathing |
|---|---|---|---|
| Minimal (anxiolysis) | Normal speech | Own | Normal |
| Moderate | Voice or light touch | Own | Adequate |
| Deep | Repeated or painful stimulus | May need help | May be inadequate |
| General anesthesia | Nothing | Needs help | Often absent |

Nobody can hold a patient reliably at one level. Drugs are titrated toward a target and patients slide a level deeper than intended regularly, which is why the room is always set up for **one level deeper than planned**.

## Before any drug is drawn

- **Consent**, documented, with the risks named by the provider.
- **Airway look:** mouth opening, neck movement, Mallampati class, beard, obesity, sleep apnea, any past difficult intubation. A hard airway changes the drug and occasionally moves the case to an operating room.
- **Fasting status.** Emergency practice does not delay an urgent procedure purely for fasting time, because delaying has not been shown to lower aspiration risk in this setting. It is still recorded and it still influences depth and drug choice.
- **ASA physical status class**, the provider's shorthand for how sick the patient is at baseline.
- **Allergies, last opioid or benzodiazepine dose, pregnancy status, weight in kilograms.**
- **Two clinicians at minimum:** one performing the procedure, one whose only job is the patient. That second person does not hold a limb, does not fetch, does not chart at the desk.

## The room, and who owns what

Suction on and tested, Yankauer tucked beside the pillow. Oxygen flowing and a bag-valve-mask connected. Oral and nasal airways out of their wrappers. Advanced airway equipment available. Monitor showing continuous pulse oximetry with the tone audible, cardiac rhythm, blood pressure cycling every `3-5 minutes`, and **waveform capnography**. IV patent, flushed and running. Reversal drugs available per policy: **naloxone `0.4 mg`** for opioids, **flumazenil `0.2 mg`** for benzodiazepines. Time-out said out loud.

Capnography earns its place here more than anywhere else in the department. A patient breathing supplemental oxygen can be completely apneic for a minute or more before the pulse oximeter moves at all, because the lungs are still full of oxygen. A flat capnogram is apnea happening right now. A climbing end-tidal number with a preserved waveform is hypoventilation, which is the warning before the flat line.

## During

Record vital signs at least every `5 minutes`, and the drug, dose, route and time of every administration. Say what you see out loud, because the person doing the procedure is looking at a shoulder and not at a monitor: "sat 93 and falling", "no waveform for three breaths", "he is snoring". A chin lift and a jaw thrust fix most events. A shoulder squeeze and a request to take a deep breath fix many of the rest.

The agents you will see, and what each one does to you:

- **Ketamine:** dissociative, preserves respiratory drive and airway reflexes better than the others, can cause laryngospasm in young children and an unpleasant emergence in adults.
- **Propofol:** on fast, off fast, drops blood pressure and causes apnea.
- **Etomidate:** hemodynamically quiet, causes myoclonus that looks alarming and is not.
- **Midazolam with fentanyl:** slower on, longer lasting, and the combination most associated with respiratory depression.

## Recovery and discharge

Sedation is not over when the procedure is over. Peak drug effect can arrive after the painful stimulus stops, which is exactly when everyone relaxes. Monitoring continues, commonly about `30 minutes` of continuous monitoring after the last dose and after the patient is awake.

The usual discharge criteria:

1. Awake and oriented to their own baseline.
2. Vital signs stable and within about `20%` of pre-procedure values.
3. Airway protected, breathing unassisted, saturation back at baseline on room air.
4. Pain and nausea controlled.
5. Able to sit, and in most departments to walk, without dizziness.
6. A responsible adult to drive and observe.
7. Written instructions: no driving, no machinery, no alcohol and no legal decisions for `24 hours`.

Two scoring tools formalize this. The **Aldrete score** rates activity, respiration, circulation, consciousness and oxygen saturation `0-2` each for a total of `10`, and `9` or more is a common threshold. The **RASS** runs from `+4` combative to `-5` unarousable, with `0` alert and calm.

> **Key:** The person watching the patient watches only the patient. The moment they are asked to hold a leg, the sedation is unmonitored.

> **Trap:** "She is satting 100 percent on oxygen" is not reassurance during sedation. That is precisely the setting where capnography catches apnea a full minute before the oximeter.
keyPoints: Set the room up for one level deeper than the sedation intended, because patients slide between levels.
Capnography detects apnea long before pulse oximetry in a patient receiving supplemental oxygen.
The dedicated monitoring person does nothing but monitor; naloxone 0.4 mg and flumazenil 0.2 mg stay available.
Monitor about 30 minutes after the last dose, because peak effect can arrive after the stimulus stops.
Discharge needs baseline mental status, stable vitals, a protected airway, a responsible adult, and 24-hour written restrictions; Aldrete 9 or more is a common bar.

checks.q: Why must the person monitoring a procedural sedation have no other assigned task?
choices: Hospital billing requires a second signature
Deterioration during sedation is fast and silent, and a monitor who is holding a limb is not watching the patient
Two people are needed to document the same vital signs
It shortens the recovery period
checks.why: Apnea, airway obstruction and hypotension develop within seconds and are caught only by someone watching. Billing, duplicate charting and recovery time have nothing to do with the rule.

checks.q: During sedation the capnogram goes flat while the pulse oximeter still reads 99% on 4 L by nasal cannula. What is happening?
choices: Artifact in the sampling line; no action needed
Apnea, which the oximeter will not reflect for another minute because of the oxygen reservoir in the lungs
The patient is hyperventilating
The monitor needs recalibration
checks.why: No exhaled carbon dioxide means no air movement. Supplemental oxygen keeps saturation high for a minute or more after breathing stops, so waiting for the oximeter wastes the safest part of the event. Hyperventilation produces a waveform with a low value, not a flat line.

checks.q: After ketamine sedation a patient is awake, oriented, vitals at baseline, no nausea, and has walked to the bathroom. What is still required before discharge?
choices: A repeat X-ray of the joint
A responsible adult to drive and observe, plus written 24-hour restrictions
An overnight observation bed
A dose of flumazenil
checks.why: Residual sedative effect outlasts an alert appearance, so a responsible adult and written restrictions on driving, machinery, alcohol and legal decisions are standard. Imaging is decided by the procedure, observation is not routine, and flumazenil does not reverse ketamine.

lessons.title: Arthrocentesis, chest tube and the drainage system
lessons.body:
## Joint aspiration (arthrocentesis)

The question is nearly always the same: is this joint infected? A hot, swollen, painful joint gets tapped because a septic joint and a gout flare look identical from the outside, and a septic joint destroys cartilage within days.

**Tray:** chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine prep, sterile drape and gloves, a `25 gauge` needle with lidocaine for the skin, an `18-20 gauge` needle for the joint, `10-20 mL` syringes and a `30-60 mL` syringe for a large effusion, a hemostat to hold the needle steady while syringes are swapped, and a dressing.

**The tubes are the part that gets done wrong.**

| Tube | Test |
|---|---|
| Sterile plain tube or culture bottles | Gram stain and culture |
| Lavender, with EDTA | Cell count and differential |
| Green (heparin) or plain, per lab policy | Crystals under polarized light |

Send them promptly. A cell count left sitting on a counter degrades and the number becomes unusable.

**Positioning:** knee straight with a small roll underneath and the patient supine; shoulder sitting with the arm resting at the side; ankle supine with the foot slightly pointed. **Never tap through cellulitis.** Pushing a needle through infected skin seeds a clean joint.

Normal joint fluid is clear, straw-colored, and you can read print through it. Cloudy, thick or frankly purulent fluid is the finding that gets the room moving.

## Chest tube (tube thoracostomy)

Air or blood has collected in the space around the lung. Air rises, so a tube for a pneumothorax sits higher and anterior. Blood sinks, so a tube for a hemothorax sits lower and posterior. Both usually enter through the **safe triangle**, bounded by the edge of the pectoralis major in front, the latissimus dorsi behind, and a line level with the nipple below, at the `4th` or `5th` intercostal space in the midaxillary line.

The tube always passes **over the top of the lower rib**, because the artery, vein and nerve run in a groove under the bottom edge of the rib above.

**What you set up:** the thoracostomy tray with scalpel, large curved clamps, suture and driver; the sizes asked for, roughly `28-36 French` for blood and `14-22 French` or a pigtail catheter for air; plenty of lidocaine, because the pleura is exquisitely sensitive; the drainage unit primed with sterile water to the fill line; suction tubing and a regulator; an occlusive dressing; and a second pair of hands. Position supine with the arm raised over the head and secured, bed tilted slightly head-up.

## The drainage system, three chambers

A modern disposable unit is one box doing three jobs.

1. **Collection chamber.** Everything drained lands here. Mark the level and the time on the outside with a pen at least every shift, and immediately after a large output. Report more than `100-200 mL per hour`, or any sudden large volume, to the nurse or provider.
2. **Water seal chamber.** A one-way valve made of water. Air can bubble out of the chest, and nothing can go back in. Two things are read here. **Tidaling** is the fluid level rising and falling with breathing, and it means the system is patent; tidaling that stops means the lung has re-expanded or the tube is blocked or kinked. **Continuous bubbling** means an air leak, expected immediately after a pneumothorax is drained, but new or persistent bubbling later means a leak somewhere in the patient or the tubing.
3. **Suction control chamber.** Sets how much negative pressure is applied, commonly `-20 cm H2O`, by a water column or a dry dial. In a water column, gentle continuous bubbling is what working suction looks like. Vigorous bubbling just evaporates the water.

Rules that do not bend: keep the unit **upright and below the level of the chest**; do not clamp a chest tube for more than a moment except when specifically ordered, because clamping a tube with an air leak can build a tension pneumothorax; do not routinely milk or strip the tubing; keep an occlusive dressing and a clamp at the bedside.

If the **tube comes out of the patient**, cover the site immediately with an occlusive dressing taped on **three sides** so air can escape but not enter, and call for help. If the **tube separates from the drainage unit**, put the free end into a bottle of sterile water to make a temporary water seal rather than leaving it open to air.

> **Key:** Tidaling means patent. Bubbling in the water seal means air is leaving the chest, whether from the lung or from a leak in your tubing.

> **Trap:** Clamping a chest tube because it is bubbling is exactly backwards. The bubbling is the tube doing its job.
keyPoints: Joint fluid splits into three tubes: culture, lavender EDTA for cell count, and a tube for crystals; never tap through cellulitis.
Chest tubes enter the safe triangle at the 4th or 5th intercostal space and always pass over the top of the lower rib.
Mark the collection chamber with volume and time; report more than 100-200 mL per hour.
Water seal: tidaling means patent, continuous bubbling means an air leak; suction is commonly set to -20 cm H2O.
A dislodged chest tube gets an occlusive dressing taped on three sides; a disconnected one goes into sterile water.

checks.q: A chest tube stops tidaling an hour after insertion. What are the two possibilities?
choices: The lung has re-expanded, or the tube is blocked or kinked
The suction is too high, or the patient is dehydrated
There is an air leak, or the collection chamber is full
The unit is above chest level, or the water seal has dried out
checks.why: Tidaling reflects pleural pressure reaching the water seal, so it stops either because there is no longer a space to transmit pressure from, or because the path is obstructed. Air leaks cause bubbling, not loss of tidaling, and hydration is irrelevant.

checks.q: Fluid is aspirated from a hot, swollen knee. Which tube is needed for the cell count and differential?
choices: Sterile plain red top
Lavender with EDTA
Blue citrate
Gray fluoride
checks.why: EDTA preserves cells for counting, which is why the lavender tube is used for a synovial cell count just as it is for a blood count. Plain tubes go for culture, citrate is for coagulation testing, and fluoride is for glucose and lactate.

checks.q: Why does a chest tube pass over the top of the rib below rather than under the rib above?
choices: The pleura is thinner there
The artery, vein and nerve run in a groove along the lower edge of each rib
It produces a smaller scar
The intercostal muscle is weaker there
checks.why: The neurovascular bundle sits tucked under the inferior margin of each rib, so hugging the upper edge of the rib below keeps the needle or tube away from it. Scar size, pleural thickness and muscle strength are not the reason.

lessons.title: Lumbar puncture, central line and arterial line: your half of the setup
lessons.body:
## Lumbar puncture

The needle passes between two lumbar spines, below where the spinal cord itself ends at about `L1-L2` in an adult, into the sac of cerebrospinal fluid. The usual target is `L3-L4` or `L4-L5`, located off a line drawn between the tops of the hip bones (iliac crests).

**The position is most of the success, and the position is yours.** Lateral decubitus, back at the very edge of the bed and perpendicular to it, hips and shoulders **stacked square** so the spine is not rotated, knees drawn toward the chest, chin tucked, back curled like a shrimp. That curl is what opens the gaps between the spines. Hold the patient there with one hand behind the neck and one behind the knees, coach their breathing, and warn before anything moves.

Sitting up and leaning forward over a table with a pillow to hug is easier to hold and better in obese patients, but **opening pressure cannot be measured sitting up**. If the provider needs a pressure, which matters in suspected idiopathic intracranial hypertension, the patient has to be lateral.

**Tray:** the prepackaged kit holds the spinal needle, commonly `20-22 gauge`, a manometer with a three-way stopcock, four numbered collection tubes, drape, prep and lidocaine. Add extra lidocaine, a stool for the provider, and a blood culture bottle if your lab takes one.

The four tubes are numbered and they are not interchangeable.

| Tube | Usual test |
|---|---|
| 1 | Cell count |
| 2 | Glucose and protein |
| 3 | Gram stain and culture |
| 4 | Cell count again, compared against tube 1 |

Tubes `1` and `4` together answer one specific question: was the blood in the fluid from the needle or from the patient? A traumatic tap clears between tube 1 and tube 4. A subarachnoid hemorrhage does not.

Afterward, the classic complication is a positional headache that is worse sitting and better lying flat. Lying flat afterward has not been shown to prevent it, but it does help once it has started.

## Central line

**What the kit does not contain:** full barrier precautions for the provider (cap, mask, sterile gown, sterile gloves, full-body drape), a mask for everyone else in the room, chlorhexidine prep, saline flushes for every lumen, a sterile ultrasound probe cover with gel inside it, a transparent dressing, and a securement device.

**Position:** internal jugular or subclavian goes supine with the head down about `15 degrees` (Trendelenburg), head turned slightly away for a neck approach. Head down does two things: it distends the vein so it is a bigger target, and it raises venous pressure at the puncture site so air cannot be sucked in and cause an air embolism. Femoral goes supine and flat with the leg slightly abducted and rotated outward.

The checklist is read out loud, and **anyone in the room can stop the procedure for a break in sterility.** That is not ceremony. Catheter-related bloodstream infection is one of the outcomes hospitals are scored on, and the bundle is hand hygiene, chlorhexidine, full barrier precautions, avoiding the femoral site where practical, and daily review of whether the line can come out.

Placement is confirmed before anything caustic runs through it: ultrasound and waveform at the bedside, plus a chest X-ray for a neck or chest line to check tip position and rule out a pneumothorax.

## Arterial line

An arterial line exists for continuous blood pressure and repeated blood gases. **Nothing is ever infused through it.**

**Before:** the modified Allen test at a radial site. Compress both the radial and ulnar arteries, have the patient clench and open the hand until the palm blanches, release the ulnar side only, and watch the color return. Return within about `5-10 seconds` means the ulnar supply can carry the hand.

**Position:** palm up, wrist extended about `30-45 degrees` over a rolled towel and taped down. Overextending kinks the artery and makes the stick harder, not easier.

**Setup:** the pressure transducer kit, a bag of saline in a pressure infuser at `300 mmHg` so a slow continuous flush keeps the catheter clear, tubing primed with no bubbles anywhere, and the transducer leveled at the **phlebostatic axis**, which is the fourth intercostal space at the midaxillary line, then zeroed to air. Leveling errors are not small: roughly `7.5 mmHg` of error for every `10 cm` the transducer sits off. Too high reads falsely low, too low reads falsely high.

> **Trap:** An arterial line that suddenly shows a beautiful low flat pressure is almost always tubing, leveling or a clot, not a patient who improved. Confirm with a cuff.

> **On shift:** Label an arterial line at both ends, clearly. A drug pushed into an artery can cost a hand.
keyPoints: LP position: lateral, hips and shoulders square, knees to chest, chin tucked; opening pressure cannot be measured sitting up.
Target the L3-L4 or L4-L5 space off the iliac crest line, safely below where the cord ends at about L1-L2.
Compare CSF tube 1 with tube 4: clearing suggests a traumatic tap, unchanged blood suggests subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Central lines need full barrier precautions and 15 degrees head down for neck or chest sites, to fill the vein and prevent air embolism.
Arterial lines never receive drugs; the transducer is leveled at the phlebostatic axis, off by about 7.5 mmHg per 10 cm of error.

checks.q: A provider needs an opening pressure on a lumbar puncture. Why can the patient not be sitting up?
choices: The needle cannot reach the space in the sitting position
A sitting column of cerebrospinal fluid gives a falsely high reading that cannot be interpreted
Sitting increases the risk of a post-procedure headache
The manometer will not attach in that position
checks.why: Opening pressure is only validated with the patient lateral, because sitting adds the height of the fluid column above the needle. The space is actually easier to enter sitting, the manometer attaches either way, and headache risk is not the issue.

checks.q: Why is a patient placed head down for internal jugular central line placement?
choices: To reduce procedural pain
To distend the vein and raise venous pressure so air cannot be entrained
To lower systemic blood pressure during the stick
To improve the ultrasound view of the lung
checks.why: Trendelenburg fills the vein, making it a larger target, and keeps pressure inside the vein above atmospheric so air embolism cannot occur at the puncture. It does not reduce pain, lower blood pressure usefully, or improve lung imaging.

checks.q: An arterial line transducer is taped to the IV pole about 20 cm above the phlebostatic axis. What happens to the displayed pressure?
choices: It reads roughly 15 mmHg too low
It reads roughly 15 mmHg too high
It is unaffected as long as the system was zeroed
The waveform disappears entirely
checks.why: A transducer above the reference point loses about 7.5 mmHg per 10 cm, so 20 cm high understates pressure by about 15 mmHg. Zeroing corrects for atmospheric pressure, not for height, and the waveform itself remains present.

lessons.title: Pediatric procedures: comfort, positioning and topical anesthesia
lessons.body:
## Fear is the presenting problem

A five-year-old with a chin laceration is not mainly a wound problem. Nearly everything that makes a pediatric procedure go badly is fear, and fear is treatable. A child held down screaming remembers it, and the next visit is worse for everyone.

Three things work, and they work together: tell the truth in small words, control the environment, and take the pain away before you start.

Age-appropriate honesty means "this will feel cold and then it will feel like a pinch" is fine, and "this will not hurt" when it will is the fastest way there is to lose a child's trust. Never promise there will be no needles when there might be. Explain right before, not `20 minutes` before, because waiting is its own torture at that age.

## Positions of comfort, not restraint

Lying a child flat on their back with adults leaning over them is the most frightening arrangement available, and it is rarely necessary.

- **Infant:** swaddled with only the limb you need left out. A pacifier plus `24%` oral sucrose, `0.5-2 mL` on the tongue about `2 minutes` before the stick, measurably reduces pain in babies under roughly `12 months`.
- **Toddler and preschooler:** upright on a parent's lap, chest to chest, legs around the parent's waist, the parent's arms hugging the child's arms down. This **comfort hold** immobilizes as well as a flat restraint and feels like a hug rather than a pin.
- **School age:** sitting up, given a job ("hold this gauze", "count with me") and a genuine choice where one exists: which arm, watch or look away, sticker or no sticker.

A **papoose board** or similar mechanical immobilizer is a last resort, never a first move, needs a documented reason, and never substitutes for anesthesia. Immobilizing a child who still feels everything is restraint, not sedation.

**Child life specialists** are trained in exactly this. Where one is available they are called early, before the first failed attempt, not after it. Distraction that actually works: bubbles, a phone video held close to the face, a light-up toy, counting, or blowing a pinwheel, which also slows the child's breathing.

## Topical anesthesia buys everything else

**LET gel** (lidocaine `4%`, epinephrine `0.1%`, tetracaine `0.5%`) is the workhorse for open wounds. `1-3 mL` is placed into and over the laceration on a cotton ball or gauze, held in place, and left for `20-30 minutes`. It often makes a small facial or scalp laceration repairable with no injection at all, and where injection is still needed the needle goes through numb skin. Most protocols keep it off mucous membranes and away from end-arterial areas such as the tip of the nose, ears, digits and genitals.

**EMLA** (lidocaine `2.5%` with prilocaine `2.5%`) works on **intact** skin for IV starts and lumbar punctures and needs `60 minutes` under an occlusive dressing for full effect. **LMX-4** (liposomal lidocaine `4%`) does much the same in about `30 minutes` without a dressing. **Vapocoolant spray** buys a few seconds of surface numbness right before a stick.

> **Key:** Twenty minutes spent on LET is faster than a wrestling match, and the repair is better because the child is still.

## What is genuinely different about children

Everything is weight-based, in kilograms, and the weight is measured, not guessed. A length-based resuscitation tape is used when a scale is not possible.

- **Fast-absorbing gut** suture is common on children's facial lacerations, so nobody has to hold a four-year-old down a second time for removal.
- Children **desaturate faster** during sedation than adults, because they consume more oxygen per kilogram and hold less reserve. Preoxygenation and capnography matter more, not less.
- **Ketamine** is generally avoided under about `3 months`, and laryngospasm is the complication to be set up for in young children.
- A crying, fighting child bleeds more and raises their own intracranial pressure. Keeping a child calm is clinical, not just kind.

> **On shift:** Give the parent a job. A parent holding a phone at the child's eye level is helping. A parent apologizing and crying at the foot of the bed is making it worse, and redirecting them is a kindness to everyone including them.
keyPoints: A comfort hold on a parent's lap immobilizes as well as flat restraint and frightens far less.
Oral sucrose 24%, 0.5-2 mL about 2 minutes before a stick, reduces pain in infants under roughly 12 months.
LET gel needs 20-30 minutes on an open wound; EMLA needs 60 minutes on intact skin, LMX-4 about 30.
Mechanical immobilizers are a last resort with a documented reason and never replace anesthesia.
Children desaturate faster during sedation, and every dose is based on a measured weight in kilograms.

checks.q: A 4-year-old needs a 2 cm forehead laceration repaired. What should be applied first?
choices: A papoose board so the repair can start immediately
LET gel into and over the wound for 20-30 minutes
EMLA cream for 60 minutes
Vapocoolant spray
checks.why: LET works on open wounds and often makes the repair painless without any injection. EMLA is for intact skin and takes an hour, vapocoolant lasts seconds, and mechanical immobilization without anesthesia is restraint, not treatment.

checks.q: Which is the best position for starting an IV in a frightened 2-year-old?
choices: Supine on the stretcher with two staff holding the arms and legs
Upright chest-to-chest on a parent's lap with the arm presented to you
Prone across the parent's knees
Sitting alone on the edge of the stretcher
checks.why: The comfort hold immobilizes the child as effectively as supine restraint while feeling like a hug, which lowers distress and movement. Supine restraint is the most frightening option, prone does not present the arm, and an unsupported toddler will move.

checks.q: An infant needs a heel stick. Which non-drug measure reliably reduces the pain?
choices: A cold pack applied for 10 minutes first
24% oral sucrose 0.5-2 mL about 2 minutes before, with a pacifier
EMLA applied 5 minutes before
Swaddling that includes the head
checks.why: Oral sucrose with non-nutritive sucking has repeatedly been shown to reduce pain response in infants under about 12 months and takes about 2 minutes to work. Cold is uncomfortable, EMLA needs a full hour, and covering an infant's head is unsafe.

lessons.title: Sending a patient to the OR, and documenting what you did
lessons.body:
## The patient going straight to surgery

Most admitted patients go to a floor. A few go from the department to an operating room, and the difference is speed: appendicitis, testicular torsion, an open fracture, a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, dead bowel, a bleeding trauma. The surgeon wants that patient upstairs with the preparation already finished.

**Nothing by mouth (NPO).** From the moment surgery becomes a possibility: no food, no drink, no ice chips, not even the sip of water for a pill. Put the sign up and tell the family, because the family is who brings the coffee. Elective fasting guidance runs roughly `2 hours` for clear liquids, `6 hours` for a light meal, and `8 hours` for a heavy or fatty one, but a true emergency operation proceeds regardless and anesthesia is simply told the last intake. **What** and **when** both go in the chart.

**Consent.** The surgeon obtains it. You may witness the signature, and witnessing means you saw the patient sign, not that you explained anything. A patient who is confused, intoxicated, or who asks a question the form does not answer gets the surgeon back, not your explanation.

**Labs and blood.** A typical set is a complete blood count, a basic metabolic panel, coagulation studies, a pregnancy test for anyone of childbearing potential, and often an ECG by age or cardiac history. The one with its own rules is the **type and screen**, which identifies ABO and Rh type and looks for antibodies; a **type and crossmatch** goes further and physically reserves units for that patient. The specimen must be labeled **at the bedside, in the patient's presence**, with the patient's own identifiers, and many hospitals add a second identity check or a dedicated blood bank band. A mislabeled blood bank tube is not a paperwork problem, it is how somebody gets the wrong blood, so it is always discarded and redrawn rather than corrected.

**Access.** Two large-bore IVs for anything that might bleed, `14-18 gauge` for trauma and obstetric hemorrhage.

**The body.** Clothing off and gown on. Jewelry and piercings out, rings taped only if they truly will not come off. Dentures out, or documented as in. Contact lenses out. Hearing aids left in until the last possible moment, then labeled. Nail polish off at least one finger for the oximeter. Do **not** shave the surgical site with a razor; hair is clipped, near the time of surgery, and usually not by you.

**Belongings.** Every item on a valuables form, signed, then either locked in the department safe or handed to a named family member with the name and time recorded. Phones and cash disappear, and the accusation lands on whoever touched the bag last.

**Site marking and handoff.** The surgeon marks the correct limb while the patient is awake and can agree with it. Allergy band on. Weight documented. Then the verbal handoff: name, age, procedure, allergies, last intake and when, last vital signs, lines and where they are, drugs given and when, pending results, and anything the patient has not yet been told.

> **Trap:** "She only had a sip of water" still changes the anesthetic plan. Report every intake, including the one you were asked not to mention.

## Documenting a procedure

Everything done at a bedside is chartable, and the standard is simple: someone who was not in the room should be able to reconstruct what happened from the note.

For anything you performed or assisted with, record the **time**; **who** performed and who assisted; that **consent and identity** were verified; the **site and side**; what was used, with sizes and lot numbers where your department tracks them; the volume and type of any fluid; **specimens** taken, how labeled, and where they went; the patient's tolerance in plain words; and the **post-procedure assessment**, which for a limb means a repeat circulation, motor and sensation check with its own time.

Specimen labeling happens at the bedside, never at the desk, with two identifiers, the source, the time and your initials. A specimen labeled in the hallway is an unlabeled specimen.

If something went wrong, chart facts and actions, not conclusions and not blame. "Patient reported numbness at 14:20, splint removed at 14:22, sensation returned, RN notified at 14:23" is a record. "The splint was too tight" is an opinion, and it belongs nowhere in a chart.

> **Key:** Time-stamped, factual, and complete enough that the next person needs no explanation from you. That is the entire standard.
keyPoints: NPO means nothing at all, and the exact last intake with its time goes in the chart even when surgery proceeds anyway.
Witnessing consent means witnessing a signature; explanation belongs to the surgeon.
Blood bank specimens are labeled at the bedside with the patient present; a mislabeled tube is discarded and redrawn, never corrected.
Belongings go on a signed valuables form to the safe or a named family member, with the time recorded.
Procedure documentation: time, who, consent, site and side, materials, specimens, tolerance, and a timed post-procedure check.

checks.q: A patient going to the OR for appendicitis says she drank half a cup of coffee an hour ago and asks you not to mention it. What do you do?
choices: Honor the request, since coffee is a clear liquid
Document what she drank and when, and report it to the team
Tell her to drink water to dilute it
Cancel the case and restart the clock at 8 hours
checks.why: Anesthesia plans airway management around aspiration risk, so the last intake and its time must be reported and charted. Hiding it endangers her, drinking more makes it worse, and an emergency case is not cancelled for fasting time.

checks.q: A type and screen tube reaches the lab with the patient's name handwritten but no second identifier. What happens?
choices: The lab adds the second identifier from the order
The specimen is discarded and a new sample is drawn
It is processed with a note in the record
It is used for the screen but not for typing
checks.why: Blood bank specimens have zero tolerance for labeling error because mislabeling is the mechanism behind fatal transfusion reactions. No lab may reconstruct identity after the fact, so the tube is rejected and the patient is redrawn.

checks.q: Which entry is proper procedure documentation?
choices: The previous tech applied the splint too tightly
Patient tolerated the procedure well
1440: volar splint applied to right wrist, fingers warm and pink, radial pulse 2+, cap refill under 2 sec, sensation intact, RN notified
Splint applied to arm
checks.why: Good documentation is timed, specific about site and side, and includes the objective post-procedure assessment. The first option is blame rather than fact, the second is vague, and the last omits side, findings and time.

cards.front: Describe the path of a coaptation splint.
cards.back: A U from high in the armpit, down the inside of the arm, around the elbow at 90 degrees, back up the outside and over the top of the shoulder. Usually 75-100 cm in an adult.

cards.front: Why must the outer limb of a coaptation splint cross the deltoid?
cards.back: The elastic wrap needs the shoulder to grip against. An outer limb stopping on the upper arm has nothing anchoring it, so the splint slides down and rotates off.

cards.front: What do side struts add to a posterior long-arm splint?
cards.back: Radial and ulnar strips alongside the posterior slab block rotation as well as bending. Used for an unstable elbow or proximal forearm when flexion control alone is not enough.

cards.front: What must go between the fingers in an ulnar gutter splint, and why?
cards.back: Padding between the ring and little fingers. Skin held against skin under a splint stays damp and macerates within a day or two.

cards.front: When is a long-arm thumb spica chosen over a short-arm one?
cards.back: When rotation must be blocked, classically a proximal scaphoid fracture. A short-arm (wrist-based) spica suits de Quervain tenosynovitis and stable thumb metacarpal injuries.

cards.front: How is a mallet finger splinted, and for how long?
cards.back: DIP joint straight or slightly hyperextended, continuously for 6-8 weeks, with the PIP left free to move. If the tip is allowed to droop even once, the clock restarts.

cards.front: What is a dorsal extension-block splint for, and at what angle?
cards.back: A volar plate injury or PIP hyperextension sprain. The PIP is blocked at 20-30 degrees of flexion so it cannot hyperextend, while flexion is still allowed.

cards.front: How is a central slip (boutonniere) injury splinted?
cards.back: The PIP joint is held straight while the DIP is left free to move. Splinting the wrong joint is the classic error.

cards.front: How is a CAM walking boot fitted correctly?
cards.back: Heel seated all the way back, straps tightened from the ankle outward, and a lift on the opposite shoe so the patient is not walking permanently crooked.

cards.front: Why does the ED usually splint rather than cast a fresh fracture?
cards.back: A cast is circumferential and squeezes a limb that is still swelling, risking compartment syndrome. Casting normally waits for orthopedic follow-up in 3-7 days once swelling peaks.

cards.front: How is cast material rolled onto the limb?
cards.back: Unrolled without tension and allowed to lie down on the limb. Pulling the roll tight is the most common cause of a cast that has to be cut off the same night.

cards.front: What is the difference between univalving and bivalving a cast?
cards.back: Univalve cuts one side and spreads it. Bivalve cuts both sides so the cast becomes two shells held by the elastic wrap, which relieves the most pressure.

cards.front: A cast is bivalved but the pain does not improve. What was missed?
cards.back: The cotton padding underneath was not cut. Intact padding is still a circumferential layer, so pressure stays up.

cards.front: What is a cast window for?
cards.back: A square cut out over a wound so it can be inspected, then taped back in place so the skin does not swell up into the opening.

cards.front: Why does a cast saw blade not cut skin?
cards.back: It oscillates through a small arc at roughly 15,000-20,000 cycles per minute rather than spinning. Rigid material cannot move with it and is cut; soft skin deflects.

cards.front: State three rules of safe cast saw technique.
cards.back: Cut in and out rather than dragging the blade, stay off bony prominences where padding is thin, and change a blade that feels hot or dull.

cards.front: Which patient is at highest risk of a cast saw burn?
cards.back: Anyone who cannot feel or report: sedated, confused, or neuropathic patients. The patient's own complaint is the main safety net.

cards.front: Why are toothed Adson forceps preferred over smooth ones for skin?
cards.back: The teeth grip with less crushing. Smooth jaws have to squeeze harder to hold the same tissue, which damages the wound edge.

cards.front: What is the difference between a cutting and a reverse cutting needle?
cards.back: Cutting puts the sharp edge on the inside of the curve, so the cut runs toward the wound edge. Reverse cutting puts it outside, so the stitch is less likely to tear out. Reverse cutting is the skin standard.

cards.front: What is a taper needle for, and why not skin?
cards.back: Round with no cutting edge; it spreads tissue apart rather than slicing. Used for bowel, vessel and fascia. It will not pass cleanly through skin.

cards.front: What does it mean that suture is swaged?
cards.back: The thread is molded into the back of the needle, so there is no eye and no doubled thread dragging through tissue.

cards.front: How many throws for nylon versus polypropylene?
cards.back: About 3-4 for nylon and 4-5 for polypropylene, which is slippery. Silk holds at about 3. More throws mean a bigger knot under thin skin.

cards.front: What makes a knot square rather than sliding?
cards.back: Reversing the wrap direction on each successive throw. Wrapping the same way twice produces a slip knot that loosens after the patient leaves.

cards.front: Why do you blot rather than wipe a wound during a repair?
cards.back: Wiping drags clot off and pulls the wound edges out of alignment. Blotting clears fluid without disturbing the repair.

cards.front: What belongs in the note after a laceration repair?
cards.back: Anesthetic drug, concentration, volume and time; irrigation fluid and volume; suture material, size and number placed; dressing; tetanus status; post-repair neurovascular check; removal date given.

cards.front: Describe correct staple removal technique.
cards.back: Slide both lower prongs of the remover fully under the crossbar, squeeze so the staple's midpoint bends down and both legs rotate up, then lift out. Never pry with a hemostat.

cards.front: When do scalp and trunk staples come out?
cards.back: Scalp at 7-10 days, trunk and limbs at 7-14 days. If the wound looks fragile, remove every other staple and add adhesive strips.

cards.front: Where are staples not used?
cards.back: The face, the hands, and any area about to be imaged. Elsewhere on scalp, trunk and limbs they are fast and effective.

cards.front: How is tissue adhesive applied correctly?
cards.back: Dry skin, hemostasis achieved, edges held together, then 3-4 thin layers painted across the closed wound extending 5-10 mm each side, about 30 seconds apart, holding 60 seconds after the last.

cards.front: Why are thin layers of skin glue better than one thick layer?
cards.back: Stacked thin layers cure fully and are stronger. A thick layer traps heat, cures unevenly, and is more likely to crack off.

cards.front: How do you keep skin glue out of the eye on a forehead repair?
cards.back: Position the head so the wound is the highest point and lay a gauze dam along the brow. Glue that reaches the eye gets petrolatum ointment and ophthalmology, never forced lid opening.

cards.front: Where does tincture of benzoin go, and where must it not?
cards.back: On intact skin 1-2 cm either side of the wound, allowed to get tacky. Never inside the wound, where it stings and causes inflammation.

cards.front: Why are adhesive strips spaced with gaps between them?
cards.back: So wound fluid can drain rather than collecting under a sealed surface. Parallel strips across the ends stop the edges curling.

cards.front: What is wound dehiscence, and what causes it?
cards.back: The wound coming apart. Causes: tension, infection, a slipped knot, sutures removed too early, steroids, diabetes, or a patient using the part.

cards.front: Name the four depths of sedation.
cards.back: Minimal (anxiolysis), moderate, deep, and general anesthesia. Patients slide between them, so the room is prepared for one level deeper than intended.

cards.front: Does an urgent procedure get delayed for fasting time?
cards.back: Not in current emergency practice, because delay has not been shown to lower aspiration risk here. The last intake is still recorded and still influences drug and depth choice.

cards.front: What is the rule about the dedicated monitoring person?
cards.back: That person watches only the patient. They do not hold a limb, fetch supplies, or chart at the desk. The moment they do, the sedation is unmonitored.

cards.front: Why does capnography beat pulse oximetry during sedation?
cards.back: A patient on supplemental oxygen can be apneic for a minute or more before saturation falls. A flat capnogram is apnea happening right now.

cards.front: What reversal agents and doses are kept available for sedation?
cards.back: Naloxone 0.4 mg for opioids and flumazenil 0.2 mg for benzodiazepines, drawn or immediately available per policy. Neither reverses ketamine, propofol or etomidate.

cards.front: Match the sedation agent to its main hazard: ketamine, propofol, etomidate.
cards.back: Ketamine: laryngospasm in young children and emergence reactions. Propofol: apnea and hypotension. Etomidate: myoclonus that looks alarming but is benign.

cards.front: How long is a patient monitored after the last sedation dose?
cards.back: Commonly about 30 minutes of continuous monitoring after the last dose and after the patient is awake, because peak effect can arrive once the painful stimulus stops.

cards.front: What is the Aldrete score, and what score allows discharge?
cards.back: Activity, respiration, circulation, consciousness and oxygen saturation, each 0-2, total 10. A score of 9 or more is the common threshold.

cards.front: What does RASS measure and what is its range?
cards.back: The Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale runs from +4 combative to -5 unarousable, with 0 alert and calm. It describes sedation depth in one number.

cards.front: Which tubes does joint fluid go into, and for what?
cards.back: Sterile plain tube or culture bottles for Gram stain and culture, lavender EDTA for cell count and differential, and a green or plain tube for crystals under polarized light.

cards.front: Why is a joint never tapped through cellulitis?
cards.back: The needle carries skin infection into a clean joint space. Septic arthritis destroys cartilage within days, so seeding it is a serious harm.

cards.front: Where is the safe triangle for chest tube insertion?
cards.back: Bounded by pectoralis major in front, latissimus dorsi behind, and a line level with the nipple below, at the 4th or 5th intercostal space in the midaxillary line.

cards.front: Why does a chest tube pass over the top of the lower rib?
cards.back: The intercostal artery, vein and nerve run in a groove under the bottom edge of each rib, so hugging the upper edge of the rib below avoids them.

cards.front: What chest tube sizes are used for blood versus air?
cards.back: Roughly 28-36 French for a hemothorax, and 14-22 French or a pigtail catheter for a simple pneumothorax.

cards.front: What does tidaling in the water seal chamber mean?
cards.back: The fluid rises and falls with breathing, which means the system is patent. Tidaling that stops means the lung has re-expanded or the tube is blocked or kinked.

cards.front: What does continuous bubbling in the water seal chamber mean?
cards.back: An air leak. Expected right after a pneumothorax is drained; new or persistent bubbling later means a leak in the patient or somewhere in the tubing.

cards.front: How much chest tube output should prompt you to speak up?
cards.back: More than 100-200 mL per hour, or any sudden large volume. Mark the collection chamber with the level and the time at least every shift.

cards.front: A chest tube pulls out of the patient. What do you do?
cards.back: Cover the site with an occlusive dressing taped on three sides so air can escape but not enter, and call for help immediately.

cards.front: Which interspace is targeted for a lumbar puncture, and why not higher?
cards.back: L3-L4 or L4-L5, found off a line between the iliac crests. The spinal cord itself ends around L1-L2, so a higher stick risks the cord.

cards.front: Describe the lateral position for a lumbar puncture.
cards.back: Back at the very edge of the bed and perpendicular to it, hips and shoulders stacked square, knees to chest, chin tucked, back curled. The curl opens the interspinous gaps.

cards.front: Why can opening pressure not be measured with the patient sitting?
cards.back: A sitting fluid column above the needle adds height and gives a falsely high, uninterpretable number. Opening pressure is validated only in the lateral position.

cards.front: What question do CSF tubes 1 and 4 answer together?
cards.back: Whether blood in the fluid came from the needle or the patient. A traumatic tap clears from tube 1 to tube 4; subarachnoid hemorrhage does not.

cards.front: What do the four CSF tubes usually go for?
cards.back: Tube 1 cell count, tube 2 glucose and protein, tube 3 Gram stain and culture, tube 4 a repeat cell count for comparison.

cards.front: Why is a patient placed head down for a neck or chest central line?
cards.back: Trendelenburg distends the vein into a bigger target and raises venous pressure at the puncture so air cannot be entrained and cause an air embolism.

cards.front: List the central line infection bundle.
cards.back: Hand hygiene, chlorhexidine skin prep, full barrier precautions, avoiding the femoral site where practical, and daily review of whether the line can be removed.

cards.front: How is the modified Allen test performed and interpreted?
cards.back: Compress radial and ulnar arteries, have the patient clench and open until the palm blanches, release the ulnar side, and watch color return. Return in about 5-10 seconds means adequate ulnar supply.

cards.front: Where is an arterial line transducer leveled, and what does an error cost?
cards.back: At the phlebostatic axis, the fourth intercostal space at the midaxillary line. Roughly 7.5 mmHg of error per 10 cm: too high reads low, too low reads high.

cards.front: What is a comfort hold and why use it?
cards.back: The child sits upright chest-to-chest on a parent's lap, legs around the waist, the parent's arms hugging the child's arms down. It immobilizes as well as flat restraint and frightens far less.

cards.front: How is oral sucrose used for infant procedures?
cards.back: 24% sucrose, 0.5-2 mL on the tongue about 2 minutes before the stick, with a pacifier. It measurably reduces pain response in infants under about 12 months.

cards.front: What is in LET gel, and how long does it need?
cards.back: Lidocaine 4%, epinephrine 0.1%, tetracaine 0.5%. Apply 1-3 mL into and over an open wound and leave it 20-30 minutes. Often removes the need for injection entirely.

cards.front: When is EMLA used instead of LET, and how long does it take?
cards.back: EMLA works on intact skin for IV starts and lumbar punctures, needing 60 minutes under an occlusive dressing. LMX-4 does similar work in about 30 minutes without a dressing.

cards.front: Where is LET gel avoided?
cards.back: On mucous membranes, and in most protocols on end-arterial areas such as the tip of the nose, the ears, the digits and the genitals, because of the vasoconstrictors in it.

cards.front: When is a papoose board appropriate?
cards.back: As a last resort with a documented reason, never as a first move and never as a substitute for anesthesia. Immobilizing a child who still feels everything is restraint, not sedation.

cards.front: Why do children desaturate faster than adults during sedation?
cards.back: They consume more oxygen per kilogram and hold less reserve in the lungs. Preoxygenation and capnography therefore matter more, not less.

cards.front: Why is fast-absorbing gut used on children's facial lacerations?
cards.back: It dissolves on its own, so nobody has to hold a frightened child down a second time for suture removal.

cards.front: What are the elective fasting times before anesthesia?
cards.back: Roughly 2 hours for clear liquids, 6 hours for a light meal, 8 hours for a heavy or fatty one. A true emergency proceeds regardless, with the last intake reported.

cards.front: What does it mean to witness a consent form?
cards.back: You saw the patient sign it. It does not mean you explained the procedure. Questions the form does not answer go back to the surgeon.

cards.front: What is the difference between a type and screen and a crossmatch?
cards.back: A type and screen identifies ABO and Rh type and looks for antibodies. A crossmatch goes further and physically reserves specific units for that patient.

cards.front: What happens to a mislabeled blood bank specimen?
cards.back: It is discarded and the patient is redrawn. Labels are never corrected after the fact, because mislabeling is the mechanism behind fatal transfusion reactions.

cards.front: How are patient belongings handled before the OR?
cards.back: Listed on a signed valuables form, then locked in the department safe or handed to a named family member with the name and time recorded.

cards.front: Name six things a procedure note must contain.
cards.back: Time, who performed and assisted, consent and identity verified, site and side, materials and sizes used, specimens and their labeling, patient tolerance, and a timed post-procedure assessment.

cards.front: How do you chart a complication?
cards.back: Facts and actions with times, not conclusions or blame. Record what the patient reported, what you did, when, and who you notified.

quiz.q: You are building a coaptation splint for a humeral shaft fracture. Where must the outer limb of the U end?
choices: At the mid-humerus, level with the fracture
At the elbow, matching the inner limb
Over the top of the shoulder, crossing the deltoid
At the wrist, so the forearm is supported
quiz.why: The elastic wrap needs the shoulder to anchor against; an outer limb ending on the arm lets the splint slide and rotate. The inner limb stops in the armpit, and the forearm is supported by the sling, not by the splint.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old has an unstable proximal ulna fracture near the elbow and the provider wants rotation blocked as well as bending. Which splint is appropriate?
choices: Posterior long-arm slab alone
Posterior long-arm with radial and ulnar side struts
Volar forearm splint
Ulnar gutter splint
quiz.why: Side struts running along both sides of the arm block supination and pronation, which a single posterior slab does not. A volar splint does not even cross the elbow, and an ulnar gutter treats metacarpal and phalangeal injuries.

quiz.q: You are applying an ulnar gutter splint for a boxer's fracture. Which step is skipped most often and causes skin breakdown?
choices: Placing padding between the ring and little fingers
Extending the wrist 20 degrees
Measuring on the uninjured arm
Folding the stockinette over the ends
