quiz.why: Two fingers held skin-to-skin inside a splint stay damp and macerate within a day or two. The other steps matter, but their failure produces a poorly positioned or rough splint, not skin loss between the fingers.

quiz.q: A 19-year-old hyperextended his index finger catching a ball. The PIP joint reduced on the field and he is now tender over the volar plate with a stable joint. Which splint is correct?
choices: Buddy tape alone for 7 days
Stack splint holding the DIP straight
Ulnar gutter with MCPs at 70-90 degrees
Dorsal extension-block splint holding the PIP at 20-30 degrees of flexion
quiz.why: An extension block prevents the hyperextension that reinjures the volar plate while still allowing flexion, which prevents stiffness. Buddy tape does not block extension, a stack splint treats mallet finger at the DIP, and a gutter is for metacarpal injuries.

quiz.q: A patient with a mallet finger returns at three weeks and mentions she takes the splint off each night to wash her hand. What does she need to be told?
choices: That is fine as long as she puts it back on
She should switch to buddy taping instead
The fingertip must never be allowed to droop; each time it does, the 6-8 week clock restarts
She should add a splint across the PIP joint as well
quiz.why: Extensor tendon healing at the DIP depends on uninterrupted extension, so any droop undoes the healing to date. Buddy taping does not hold extension, and splinting the PIP causes stiffness without helping the DIP.

quiz.q: Why is cast material unrolled onto the limb without tension?
choices: Pulling the roll tight makes the cast circumferentially constricting, which is the common cause of a cast that must be cut off
Tension causes the plaster to set too slowly
Tension makes the cast weaker and more likely to crack
Tension prevents the layers from laminating together
quiz.why: A cast applied under tension acts like a tourniquet as the limb swells. Setting time depends on water temperature, not tension, and a tight cast is if anything mechanically stronger, which is exactly the problem.

quiz.q: Six hours after a short-arm cast is applied, a patient has severe pain, numb fingers and pain when you gently straighten them. The cast is univalved and nothing changes. What is the next step?
choices: Reassure him and recheck in an hour
Bivalve the cast and cut the padding underneath as well
Elevate the arm and apply ice over the cast
Give oral analgesia and discharge with return precautions
quiz.why: These are compartment syndrome findings and pressure has to come off now. Bivalving with the padding cut relieves the most pressure; intact padding is still a constricting layer. Elevation, ice and analgesia delay definitive relief.

quiz.q: An 82-year-old with dementia and diabetic neuropathy is having a forearm cast removed with the saw. Which factor most increases her risk of a burn?
choices: Her age alone
The cast is fiberglass rather than plaster
Her forearm is thin
She cannot reliably feel the blade or report that it is hot
quiz.why: The patient's own complaint is the primary protection against a saw burn, and neither dementia nor neuropathy allows it. Age alone, material type and limb size do not determine burn risk the way absent sensation and reporting do.

quiz.q: A plaster short-leg cast was applied two hours ago and the patient asks when he can walk on it. What do you tell him?
choices: Immediately, since it feels hard
After one hour of elevation
Not for 24-48 hours, while the plaster reaches full strength
Not until the follow-up visit in 7 days
quiz.why: Plaster feels firm within 15 minutes but does not reach full strength for a day or more, so early weight bearing deforms or cracks it. Fiberglass is near full strength in about 30 minutes, which is a common point of confusion.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of cutting a window in a cast?
choices: To allow a wound underneath to be inspected and dressed, with the piece taped back so skin does not swell into the gap
To reduce the weight of the cast for an elderly patient
To relieve circumferential pressure across the whole limb
To allow the cast to be removed more easily later
quiz.why: A window is for access to a specific spot. Pressure relief across the limb requires univalving or bivalving. Weight and eventual removal are not the reason, and an untaped window lets skin herniate and swell into the hole.

quiz.q: Which needle point is the standard choice for closing a skin laceration?
choices: Taper
Reverse cutting
Blunt
Conventional cutting
quiz.why: Reverse cutting puts the cutting edge on the outside of the curve so the cut runs away from the wound edge and the stitch resists tearing out. Conventional cutting does the opposite, and taper and blunt needles will not pass through skin.

quiz.q: A provider trying to close a scalp laceration says the needle will not pass through the skin. You look at the packet and see a taper needle. What is the explanation?
choices: The needle is dull and needs replacing with another of the same type
The suture is too small for scalp
A taper needle has no cutting edge and spreads tissue rather than cutting it, so it is not made for skin
The wound needs more local anesthetic
quiz.why: Taper needles are round-bodied and designed for bowel, vessel and fascia. No amount of force or anesthetic makes one suitable for skin; the fix is a reverse cutting needle. Suture size affects strength, not penetration.

quiz.q: While tying, you wrap the suture around the driver in the same direction on two consecutive throws. What have you produced?
choices: A surgeon's knot
A stronger square knot
A buried dermal knot
A sliding knot that can loosen after the patient leaves
quiz.why: Squaring a knot requires reversing the wrap direction each throw. Same-direction wraps create a slip knot. A surgeon's knot is a doubled first throw, and a buried dermal knot describes placement rather than knot geometry.

quiz.q: During a facial laceration repair the field keeps filling with blood and the provider asks you to keep it clear. Which action best preserves the repair?
choices: Blot the field with gauze without dragging across the wound edges
Wipe firmly along the length of the wound
Irrigate continuously with saline while the provider sews
Apply hydrogen peroxide to stop the ooze
quiz.why: Blotting removes blood without stripping clot or pulling the edges out of alignment. Wiping displaces the edges, continuous irrigation floats the field and obscures it, and peroxide destroys healing tissue and never goes in a wound.

quiz.q: Which instrument is correct for handling the skin edge during a laceration repair?
choices: Smooth Adson forceps
Toothed Adson forceps
A hemostat
Suture scissors
quiz.why: Teeth grip skin with minimal squeeze, so the edge is not crushed. Smooth forceps must clamp harder to hold the same tissue, a hemostat crushes deliberately, and scissors are for thread.

quiz.q: You are removing staples from a healed abdominal wound. Which technique is correct?
choices: Grip the crossbar with a hemostat and pull straight up
Cut each crossbar with suture scissors and pull the legs out one at a time
Slide both lower prongs of the remover fully under the crossbar, squeeze, and lift out
Rock the staple back and forth until it loosens, then pull
quiz.why: Squeezing the remover bends the staple's midpoint downward, rotating both legs vertically so they exit their own tracks. Pulling, cutting or rocking drags the legs sideways through skin, which tears and hurts.

quiz.q: A 6 cm scalp laceration was stapled eight days ago. At recheck it is healed except for one end that looks thin and slightly separated. What is reasonable?
choices: Remove all the staples and discharge
Remove every other staple, place adhesive strips, and arrange a recheck
Leave all staples for another week
Replace the staples with sutures
quiz.why: Staggered removal keeps support on a fragile segment while starting the process, and strips add reinforcement. Taking them all risks dehiscence, leaving them all past 10 days on a scalp risks track marks and infection, and restapling a healing wound is not indicated.

quiz.q: A 5 cm laceration crosses the front of the knee and gapes open whenever the knee bends. Which closure is appropriate?
choices: Sutures, because the wound is under tension across a moving joint
Tissue adhesive, because it is a clean wound
Adhesive strips with benzoin
No closure; allow it to heal open
quiz.why: Tension is the single variable that defeats both glue and strips, and a joint adds motion on top of it. A clean wound still needs the closure strength that only sutures provide here. Leaving a gaping wound open would scar badly and heal slowly.

quiz.q: A laceration just above the eyebrow is being closed with tissue adhesive. Which single measure most reduces the risk of the worst complication?
choices: Applying a single thick layer to set faster
Applying antibiotic ointment over the glue afterward
Irrigating the wound again immediately after gluing
Positioning the head so the wound is the highest point and laying a gauze dam along the brow
quiz.why: Adhesive running into the eye is the feared complication near the brow, and gravity plus a physical dam prevents it. A thick layer is weaker than several thin ones, and ointment or water after application dissolves the glue.

quiz.q: A patient returns 48 hours after abscess drainage. Redness now extends 6 cm beyond the wound, the area is warm and tender, and his temperature is 38.4 C. What does this represent?
choices: The expected inflammatory response to packing
Spreading infection requiring provider reassessment and likely antibiotics
Wound dehiscence
A reaction to the iodoform packing strip
quiz.why: Redness spreading well beyond the wound with warmth and fever is cellulitis, not local inflammation, which stays within a centimetre or two and settles. Dehiscence means separated edges, and packing reactions do not cause fever.

quiz.q: Three days after a thigh laceration repair a patient returns with dusky skin around the wound, crackling under the skin, pain far out of proportion to the appearance, a temperature of 39.2 C and a blood pressure of 88/50. What is the priority?
choices: Remove the sutures and pack the wound
Apply warm compresses and recheck in 24 hours
Treat this as a necrotizing soft tissue infection: alert the team now and begin resuscitation
Take a wound culture and send him home on antibiotics
quiz.why: Crepitus, dusky skin, disproportionate pain and shock define a necrotizing infection, which is a surgical emergency measured in hours. Packing, compresses and outpatient antibiotics all lose time the patient does not have.

quiz.q: Why must the person monitoring a procedural sedation have no other assigned task?
choices: Deterioration is fast and silent, and a monitor who is holding a limb is not watching the patient
Two signatures are required for billing
It allows the vital signs to be charted twice for accuracy
It shortens the required recovery period
quiz.why: Apnea, obstruction and hypotension appear within seconds and are caught only by continuous observation. Documentation, billing and recovery time have nothing to do with the requirement.

quiz.q: During sedation for a shoulder reduction the capnogram goes flat for three breath cycles while the pulse oximeter still reads 99% on 4 L by nasal cannula. What is happening?
choices: The sampling line is disconnected; no clinical action is needed
The patient is apneic, and the oximeter has not fallen yet because of the oxygen reservoir in the lungs
The patient is hyperventilating
The patient is in laryngospasm with complete obstruction and needs immediate intubation
quiz.why: No exhaled carbon dioxide means no air movement, and supplemental oxygen delays desaturation by a minute or more. The first move is stimulation and a jaw thrust, not intubation. Hyperventilation produces a waveform with a low value, not a flat trace.

quiz.q: A patient becomes over-sedated after midazolam. Which reversal agent and dose should be available?
choices: Naloxone 0.4 mg
Glucagon 1 mg
Atropine 0.5 mg
Flumazenil 0.2 mg
quiz.why: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines; naloxone reverses opioids. Glucagon is used for beta blocker toxicity and atropine for symptomatic bradycardia, neither of which is a benzodiazepine reversal.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old sedated with ketamine suddenly makes a high-pitched crowing sound, the chest is not rising, and the saturation begins to fall. What is the most likely event?
choices: Emergence reaction
Myoclonus
Laryngospasm
Aspiration of gastric contents
quiz.why: Laryngospasm is the classic ketamine complication in young children and presents as stridor or silence with no air movement. Emergence reactions occur on waking and involve agitation, myoclonus is muscle jerking with intact breathing, and aspiration usually follows vomiting.

quiz.q: The reduction is finished and the room relaxes. Five minutes later the patient's saturation falls to 86%. Why is this predictable rather than surprising?
choices: Peak drug effect can arrive after the painful stimulus that was keeping the patient aroused is removed
Sedative drugs accumulate in the muscle and release when the limb is moved
Oxygen demand rises after a procedure ends
The monitor loses accuracy once the procedure is over
quiz.why: Pain is a powerful respiratory stimulant, so removing it unmasks the drug. That is exactly why monitoring continues about 30 minutes after the last dose. The other explanations are not real physiology.

quiz.q: A patient after propofol sedation is alert, oriented, vitals at baseline, walked to the bathroom and has no nausea. What still stands between her and discharge?
choices: A repeat set of laboratory studies
A responsible adult to drive and observe her, plus written 24-hour restrictions
Two more hours of observation regardless of her status
A dose of flumazenil to ensure full reversal
quiz.why: Residual effect outlasts an alert appearance, so a responsible adult and written restrictions on driving, machinery, alcohol and legal decisions are standard. Labs are not routine, fixed observation periods are not required once criteria are met, and flumazenil does not reverse propofol.

quiz.q: Three hours after chest tube placement for a pneumothorax, the water seal chamber bubbles continuously and the patient's subcutaneous emphysema is spreading up the neck. What does this suggest?
choices: Normal resolution of the pneumothorax
An ongoing air leak that needs immediate provider assessment
The suction is set too low
The collection chamber is full
quiz.why: Persistent bubbling plus expanding subcutaneous air means air is escaping somewhere it should not, from the lung or from a side hole sitting outside the pleura. Resolution reduces bubbling; suction level and chamber volume do not cause subcutaneous emphysema.

quiz.q: A new tech clamps a bubbling chest tube to quiet the noise it is making. What is the danger?
choices: The collection chamber will overflow
The tube will clot and need replacement
Air can no longer escape the chest, so a tension pneumothorax can build
The water seal will dry out
quiz.why: Bubbling means air is leaving the chest. Clamping traps it, and trapped air under pressure collapses the lung and shifts the mediastinum. Clotting and chamber volume are slower problems, and the water seal is unaffected by clamping.

quiz.q: A confused patient pulls his chest tube out of his chest. What is your immediate action?
choices: Reinsert the tube through the same site
Leave the site open so air can escape freely
Apply a dry gauze dressing taped on all four sides
Cover the site with an occlusive dressing taped on three sides and call for help
quiz.why: A three-sided occlusive dressing lets air out of the chest while preventing it being drawn in, which is the flutter-valve principle. Leaving it open allows an open pneumothorax, a fully sealed dressing can create tension, and reinsertion is not a tech procedure.

quiz.q: Fluid is aspirated from a hot, swollen knee. Which tube must the cell count and differential go into?
choices: Lavender with EDTA
Blue citrate
Gray with fluoride
Gold serum separator
quiz.why: EDTA preserves cells for counting, which is why the lavender tube is used for synovial cell counts just as for blood counts. Citrate is for coagulation, fluoride preserves glucose, and a gel separator tube is unsuitable for cell work.

quiz.q: A patient has a hot swollen knee, and the skin over the usual lateral approach is red, warm and clearly cellulitic. The provider still needs joint fluid. What should you anticipate?
choices: The tap will be abandoned entirely
A different puncture site will be chosen, because a needle must not pass through infected skin into a joint
The skin will be injected with antibiotic first
The tap will proceed through the cellulitis after extra chlorhexidine
quiz.why: Passing a needle through infected skin can seed a joint that was not septic, so an uninvolved approach is selected. The clinical question is too important to abandon, and no amount of prep or local antibiotic makes infected skin a safe entry point.

quiz.q: A chest tube placed for a traumatic hemothorax drains 450 mL in the first hour and another 220 mL in the second. What should you do?
choices: Mark the chamber and report it at the end of your shift
Milk the tubing to keep it from clotting
Report the hourly output to the nurse and provider immediately
Clamp the tube to slow the blood loss
quiz.why: Ongoing output above roughly 100-200 mL per hour is a surgical trigger and has to be communicated in real time. Waiting hides it, milking is not recommended routinely, and clamping a chest tube to reduce output is dangerous and does not stop bleeding.

quiz.q: A provider is struggling to find the interspace during a lateral lumbar puncture. You notice the patient's top shoulder has rolled forward toward the bed. What should you correct?
choices: Restack the hips and shoulders square so the spine is not rotated
Extend the patient's neck to open the airway
Straighten the knees to lengthen the spine
Move the patient to the middle of the bed
quiz.why: A rotated spine turns the target into a moving, angled slot. Squaring the hips and shoulders and keeping the back curled is what opens the interspaces. Extending the neck and straightening the knees both close them, and the patient belongs at the edge of the bed, not the middle.

quiz.q: A patient with suspected idiopathic intracranial hypertension needs an opening pressure measured. She is obese and much easier to position sitting up. What must happen?
choices: Perform the tap sitting and subtract an estimated correction
Perform the tap sitting and report the number as measured
Defer the opening pressure and send fluid studies only
Perform the tap in the lateral position, because opening pressure is only valid lying on the side
quiz.why: Sitting adds the height of the fluid column above the needle, so the number cannot be interpreted and no validated correction exists. If the pressure is the reason for the tap, the patient has to be lateral, however awkward.

quiz.q: Cerebrospinal fluid tube 1 contains 4,000 red cells per microlitre and tube 4 contains 120. What does this pattern suggest?
choices: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
A traumatic tap, with blood introduced by the needle clearing as fluid is collected
Bacterial meningitis
A laboratory error requiring a repeat tap
quiz.why: Blood from the needle track washes out across the tubes, so counts fall sharply from tube 1 to tube 4. In subarachnoid hemorrhage the blood is already mixed throughout and the counts stay similar. Cell counts do not diagnose meningitis by themselves.

quiz.q: Why is a patient positioned head down about 15 degrees for internal jugular central line placement?
choices: To reduce the pain of the local anesthetic
To lower the patient's blood pressure during the puncture
To distend the vein and raise venous pressure so air cannot be entrained
To improve the ultrasound image of the carotid artery
quiz.why: Trendelenburg fills the vein, making it a larger target, and keeps intravenous pressure above atmospheric so air embolism cannot occur at the puncture. It does not affect pain, is not used to alter blood pressure, and does not improve arterial imaging.

quiz.q: A hypotensive patient has an arterial line and one peripheral IV that has just infiltrated. A nurse asks you to push a saline bolus through the arterial line. What is the correct response?
choices: Nothing is ever infused through an arterial line; new venous access is needed
Push it slowly, since saline is not caustic
Push it only if the line was placed under ultrasound
Push it after disconnecting the transducer
quiz.why: Arterial lines exist for monitoring and sampling only. Injecting into an artery can cause distal ischemia and limb loss, and that risk does not change with the fluid, the technique or how the line was placed.

quiz.q: An arterial line reads 78/44 while a cuff on the opposite arm reads 118/70. The patient is alert, warm and well perfused. What should you check first?
choices: Give a fluid bolus for the low arterial reading
Remove the arterial line as unreliable
Recheck the cuff on the same arm as the line
Check that the transducer is level at the phlebostatic axis and zeroed, and inspect the tubing for bubbles or a clot
quiz.why: A well-perfused patient with a discrepant tracing almost always has a system problem: transducer too high, not zeroed, or damped tubing. Treating the number would be treating an artifact, and the line is fixable rather than disposable.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old has a 2 cm forehead laceration that needs repair. What should be applied first?
choices: Vapocoolant spray immediately before injection
LET gel into and over the wound for 20-30 minutes
EMLA cream over the wound for 60 minutes
A papoose board so the repair can begin right away
quiz.why: LET works on open wounds and often makes a small facial laceration repairable without any injection. EMLA is for intact skin and takes an hour, vapocoolant lasts seconds, and mechanical immobilization without anesthesia is restraint rather than treatment.

quiz.q: A frightened 2-year-old needs an IV. Which approach is most likely to succeed on the first attempt?
choices: Supine on the stretcher with two staff holding the arms and legs
Prone across a parent's knees
Upright chest-to-chest on the parent's lap with the arm presented to you
Seated alone on the edge of the stretcher with a sticker as a reward
quiz.why: The comfort hold immobilizes as effectively as supine restraint while feeling like a hug, so the child moves less and the stick succeeds. Supine restraint is the most frightening arrangement, prone does not present the arm, and an unsupported toddler will pull away.

quiz.q: Which non-drug measure reliably reduces pain during a heel stick in a 3-month-old?
choices: 24% oral sucrose 0.5-2 mL about 2 minutes before, with a pacifier
A cold pack applied to the heel for 10 minutes
Vapocoolant spray to the heel
Holding the infant's head still
quiz.why: Oral sucrose with non-nutritive sucking has repeatedly reduced pain response in infants under about 12 months and needs roughly 2 minutes to take effect. Cold is itself uncomfortable, vapocoolant is not used routinely on infant heels, and head restraint does nothing for pain.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old will need an IV for antibiotics in about 90 minutes and the skin is intact. Which topical option best fits the time available?
choices: LET gel applied to the intended IV site
Vapocoolant spray at the time of the stick
Injected lidocaine at the site 60 minutes early
EMLA under an occlusive dressing for 60 minutes
quiz.why: EMLA works on intact skin and reaches full effect at about an hour, which fits the window. LET is for open wounds, vapocoolant gives only seconds of surface numbness, and injecting lidocaine to prevent the pain of a needle defeats the purpose.

quiz.q: A frightened 5-year-old needs a chin laceration repaired, and someone suggests going straight to a papoose board. What is the problem with that plan?
choices: Papoose boards are never permitted in any setting
It is a last resort, it provides no anesthesia, and comfort positioning plus topical anesthetic should come first
It requires a provider order that cannot be obtained quickly
It will contaminate the sterile field
quiz.why: Mechanical immobilization holds a child who still feels everything, which is restraint rather than treatment. It is permitted as a documented last resort, but LET, a comfort hold, distraction and child life come first.

quiz.q: A patient going to the operating room for appendicitis tells you she drank half a cup of coffee an hour ago and asks you not to mention it. What do you do?
choices: Honor the request, since coffee is a clear liquid
Tell her to drink water to dilute it
Document what she drank and when, and report it to the team
Cancel the case and restart an 8-hour fasting clock
quiz.why: Anesthesia plans airway management around aspiration risk, so the type and timing of the last intake must be reported and charted. Concealing it endangers her, more fluid makes it worse, and an emergency operation is not delayed for fasting time.

quiz.q: A type and screen specimen arrives in the blood bank with the patient's name written on it but no second identifier and no collector initials. What happens next?
choices: The specimen is discarded and a new sample is drawn
The laboratory adds the missing identifiers from the electronic order
It is processed with a note documenting the discrepancy
It is used to determine type but not to screen for antibodies
quiz.why: Blood bank specimens have zero tolerance for labeling error, because mislabeling is the mechanism behind fatal transfusion reactions. Identity can never be reconstructed after the fact, so the tube is rejected and the patient is redrawn.

quiz.q: You are asked to witness a surgical consent. As the patient signs, she asks you what the risks of the operation actually are. What is correct?
choices: Explain the common risks you know for that operation
Tell her the surgeon already covered it and have her sign
Decline to witness and leave the form unsigned
Stop, and ask the surgeon to return and answer her question before the form is completed
quiz.why: Witnessing attests to the signature, not to the explanation, and an unanswered question means informed consent is incomplete. Explaining risks yourself exceeds scope, brushing her off invalidates the consent, and simply walking away leaves the problem unaddressed.

quiz.q: A patient in a new forearm splint reports numbness at 14:20. You remove the splint, sensation returns, and you notify the nurse. Which chart entry is appropriate?
choices: Splint was applied too tightly by the previous shift
1420 patient reported numbness in right fingers; splint removed 1422; sensation returned; radial pulse 2+; RN notified 1423
Patient complained; issue resolved
Neurovascular compromise secondary to improper splint application
quiz.why: Documentation records timed facts and actions so another clinician can reconstruct events. The other options assign blame, state a conclusion the record cannot support, or omit the times and findings that make the note useful.

quiz.q: Where must a blood bank specimen be labeled?
choices: At the bedside, in the patient's presence, immediately after the draw
At the nursing station using the printed label sheet
In the laboratory receiving area
Anywhere, as long as two identifiers are used
quiz.why: Labeling away from the patient breaks the chain that links tube to person, which is exactly how wrong-blood-in-tube errors occur. Two identifiers are necessary but not sufficient; the location and timing of labeling matter just as much.

scenarios.title: Room 12: 6-year-old, chin laceration, terrified
scenarios.intro: Triage sends back a 6-year-old who fell off a scooter and split his chin open. He is crying, clinging to his mother, and pulling away from anyone in scrubs. The laceration is `2 cm`, clean edges, no through-and-through injury to the mouth. The provider says she will repair it when the room is ready. You are the tech assigned.

steps.prompt:
He screams when you come near with a penlight. His mother looks close to tears herself. The provider is finishing another patient and will be about `25 minutes`.

What do you do with those 25 minutes?

choices.text: Get LET gel on the wound now so it has the full 20-30 minutes to work, and bring the mother onto the bed with him
choices.feedback: Exactly right. The waiting time is the anesthetic time. LET applied now means the repair may need no injection at all, and the child is calmer because a parent is holding him rather than staff pinning him.

choices.text: Set up the suture tray first and deal with the child when the provider arrives
choices.feedback: The tray takes two minutes and can happen anytime. The clock that matters is the 20-30 minutes LET needs, and you just spent it on a task that did not need doing yet.

choices.text: Ask for a papoose board so he can be held still as soon as the provider is free
choices.feedback: This is the wrong first move. Mechanical immobilization gives no pain relief at all, it is a documented last resort, and it makes every future visit worse. Topical anesthesia and a comfort hold come first.

choices.text: Tell him firmly that it will not hurt at all and that big kids do not cry
choices.feedback: Two problems. It will hurt somewhat, so you have promised something you cannot deliver and will lose his trust the moment you are wrong, and shaming a frightened child escalates rather than settles him.

steps.prompt:
LET is on, held in place on a gauze pad by his mother's gloved hand. He has stopped screaming and is watching a video on her phone. Child life is available in the department today.

The provider arrives and asks how you want to position him.

choices.text: Upright on his mother's lap, chest to chest, her arms around his arms, head steadied against her shoulder
choices.feedback: The comfort hold. It immobilizes the head and arms as well as a flat restraint and feels like a hug, and a chin wound is well exposed with the head tipped back on the parent's shoulder.

choices.text: Supine on the stretcher with you holding his shoulders and another tech holding his legs
choices.feedback: This is the most frightening arrangement available and it costs you the cooperation the LET just bought. Save flat restraint for when a comfort hold has genuinely failed.

choices.text: Sitting on the stretcher alone with a sticker as a reward for holding still
choices.feedback: A six-year-old's best intentions do not survive the first instrument near his face. He needs physical support from a trusted adult, not a promise.

choices.text: Call child life to come sit with him for distraction while you position him on his mother's lap
choices.feedback: Very good. Child life plus a comfort hold is the combination with the best odds, and calling them before the first attempt rather than after a failure is the right timing.

steps.prompt:
The provider tests the wound edge with forceps. He does not flinch. She says the LET has worked and she will not need to inject.

She asks what suture you have pulled for a child's chin.

choices.text: 5-0 nylon, with removal in 5 days
choices.feedback: Reasonable size and a defensible plan, but it books this child a second visit and a second round of fear for removal. There is a better option on the shelf.

choices.text: 5-0 fast-absorbing gut, so nothing has to be removed
choices.feedback: The better choice for a child's face. It dissolves on its own, which means nobody has to hold him down a second time, and cosmetic results on the face are comparable.

choices.text: 3-0 nylon, since the chin takes tension when he talks
choices.feedback: Far too thick for a face. A 3-0 on a child's chin leaves visible suture marks. Face is 6-0 to 5-0 territory.

choices.text: Staples, because they are quick and he is squirming
choices.feedback: Staples are never used on the face. Speed does not justify the scar, and this wound is already anesthetized and still.

steps.prompt:
The repair takes four minutes. He watched the whole video and did not move. His mother asks what happens at home, and whether he will have a scar.

What are the discharge instructions?

choices.text: Keep it clean and dry for 24-48 hours, then gentle washing; the gut sutures fall out on their own; sun protection on the scar for months; return for spreading redness, pus, fever or the wound opening
choices.feedback: Complete. Wound care, the fact that nothing needs removing, realistic scar expectations with sun protection, and specific return precautions rather than a vague instruction to watch it.

choices.text: Apply antibiotic ointment three times a day and cover it with a bandage for a week
choices.feedback: Heavy ointment on absorbable gut on the face is not necessary, and a week of occlusive covering on a child's chin macerates the skin. Keep it simple.

choices.text: Tell her the sutures come out in five days at the pediatrician
choices.feedback: This is the wrong instruction for absorbable gut and it sends a frightened child for a procedure he does not need. Confirm what was used before you give removal instructions.

choices.text: Have her scrub the wound daily with hydrogen peroxide to prevent infection
choices.feedback: Peroxide destroys healing cells and dissolves nothing useful. It has no place on a fresh repair, at home or in the department.

scenarios.debrief:
The wound was never the hard part. Everything that made this repair succeed happened before the provider sat down: LET applied the moment the plan was known so the waiting room time became the anesthetic time, a parent used as the immobilizer instead of staff, child life called before the first failure rather than after it, and a suture chosen so the child never has to come back for a second frightening visit. The pattern to carry: in pediatrics, anesthesia and positioning are the procedure. Get those two right and the technical part is usually easy.

The traps in this case are the ones that look efficient. Setting up the tray first, restraining early, promising no pain, and choosing the suture you always use are all small decisions that each cost the child something, and together they turn a four-minute repair into a wrestling match.

scenarios.title: Trauma 2: chest tube for a hemothorax
scenarios.intro: A 34-year-old restrained driver arrives after a side-impact collision. He is talking, in pain, with decreased breath sounds on the left and a chest X-ray showing a large left hemothorax. The attending says she wants a `32 French` tube in the left chest now and asks you to set it up.

steps.prompt:
You have about two minutes while she gowns up.

What do you set up, and how do you position him?

choices.text: Thoracostomy tray, 32 French tube, plenty of lidocaine, drainage unit primed with sterile water to the fill line, suction tubing and regulator, occlusive dressing; patient supine with the left arm raised above his head and secured, bed tilted slightly head-up
choices.feedback: Complete. The primed drainage unit is the item most often forgotten until the tube is already in, and priming it after the fact wastes time at exactly the wrong moment. The raised arm opens the axilla and exposes the safe triangle.

choices.text: Tray and tube only; the drainage system can be connected once the tube is in
choices.feedback: You will be priming a water seal with a chest tube hanging open in a trauma bay. Prime it before, every time.

choices.text: Tray, tube and drainage unit, with the patient sitting fully upright so he can breathe more comfortably
choices.feedback: Good equipment, wrong position. Sitting fully upright closes the axilla and makes the safe triangle hard to reach. Supine with the arm raised, slightly head-up, is the working position.

choices.text: Tray, tube and a chest drain unit primed with saline rather than sterile water
choices.feedback: The water seal is meant to be filled with sterile water to the marked line. Substituting a different fluid changes the seal and is not how the device is validated.

steps.prompt:
She preps and drapes, then infiltrates generously. As she makes the incision she says out loud, "Fifth intercostal space, midaxillary line, and I am walking over the top of the rib."

A student watching asks you why she is going over the top of the rib instead of under the one above.

choices.text: Because the pleura is thinner at the top of each rib space
choices.feedback: Not the reason. Pleural thickness is not the issue and this explanation would leave the student with the wrong mental model.

choices.text: Because the intercostal artery, vein and nerve run in a groove under the lower edge of each rib, so hugging the upper edge of the rib below avoids them
choices.feedback: Correct and it is the whole reason. The neurovascular bundle is tucked under the inferior margin, which is why every needle or tube into the chest rides the top of the lower rib.

choices.text: Because it leaves a smaller scar
choices.feedback: Cosmetic outcome has nothing to do with it. The rule exists to avoid bleeding and nerve injury.

choices.text: Because the lung sits higher in the space at that level
choices.feedback: Not correct, and it invents anatomy. The rule is entirely about the neurovascular bundle under each rib.

steps.prompt:
The tube goes in and immediately drains dark blood. You connect it to the primed unit and place it on `-20 cm H2O` of suction. Within ten minutes the collection chamber reads `480 mL`. The water seal is tidaling well with his breathing and there is no bubbling.

What do you do?

choices.text: Mark the chamber with the level and the time, and tell the attending the output now, out loud
choices.feedback: Right. Nearly 500 mL in the first ten minutes with a rising heart rate and falling pressure is a number the surgical decision depends on, and it has to be said now, not at handoff.

choices.text: Mark the chamber and note the volume for your end-of-shift report
choices.feedback: Marking is correct, timing is not. This is an actionable number in a trauma bay and it cannot wait for a report.

choices.text: Clamp the tube briefly to slow the bleeding while you tell someone
choices.feedback: Clamping does not stop bleeding into the chest, it only hides it and can build pressure. Never clamp to control output.

choices.text: Check that the unit is upright and below the level of his chest, mark the level and time, and report the output immediately
choices.feedback: Also correct, and the position check is a good habit. A unit lifted above chest level can allow drainage back toward the patient and stops reading accurately.

steps.prompt:
The attending is now on the phone with the operating room. Twenty minutes later you notice the water seal has stopped tidaling entirely, and the drainage has slowed to a trickle even though he still looks pale and his heart rate is `124`.

What does this mean and what do you do?

choices.text: The bleeding has stopped; document the improvement
choices.feedback: This is the dangerous reading. He looks worse, not better, so loss of drainage with a deteriorating patient means the tube is not working, not that the problem resolved.

choices.text: Loss of tidaling means the lung has re-expanded or the tube is blocked or kinked; check the tubing for clot, kinks and the patient lying on it, and report it immediately
choices.feedback: Exactly. Two possibilities, and with a deteriorating patient you assume obstruction until proven otherwise. A clotted tube in a hemothorax is a patient bleeding into a space with no way out.

choices.text: Strip and milk the tubing vigorously until flow returns
choices.feedback: Routine stripping is not recommended and generates very high negative pressures inside the chest. Inspect, unkink, reposition, and escalate instead.

choices.text: Increase the suction to -40 cm H2O to pull the clot through
choices.feedback: Higher suction does not clear a clot and is not a setting you change on your own. The problem is mechanical and it needs a provider looking at it.

scenarios.debrief:
Two ideas carried this whole case. The first is that the drainage unit is prepared before the tube exists, because there is no good moment to prime a water seal with an open chest in front of you. The second is that the three chambers are a set of readings, not decoration: the collection chamber is a number you mark, time and report out loud when it crosses roughly 100-200 mL per hour; the water seal tells you whether the system is patent (tidaling) and whether air is escaping (bubbling); and the suction chamber tells you the pressure being applied.

The trap at the end is the one that catches people. Drainage stopping is good news only if the patient is getting better. In a patient whose heart rate is climbing and whose pressure is falling, a tube that stops draining is an obstructed tube until somebody proves otherwise.

scenarios.title: Room 3: sedation for an anterior shoulder reduction
scenarios.intro: A 41-year-old man dislocated his right shoulder playing hockey two hours ago. Films confirm an anterior dislocation with no fracture. The provider plans procedural sedation with propofol and asks you to get the room ready and monitor. He last ate a sandwich `90 minutes` ago.

steps.prompt:
The provider is drawing up drugs. You are setting the room.

Which setup is complete?

choices.text: Monitor with pulse oximetry and cardiac rhythm, blood pressure cycling every 3-5 minutes, IV patent
choices.feedback: Most of the way there and still missing the monitor that matters most for this drug, plus the rescue equipment. Propofol causes apnea, and you have no way to see it early.

choices.text: Suction on and tested with the Yankauer at the head, oxygen and a bag-valve-mask connected, airway adjuncts unwrapped, monitor with pulse oximetry, rhythm, cycling blood pressure and waveform capnography, IV patent, reversal agents available, time-out done
choices.feedback: Complete. Note that the room is set for one level deeper than intended, because patients slide. Capnography is the item that will earn its place in about four minutes.

choices.text: Everything above, but skip capnography since he will be on supplemental oxygen and the pulse oximeter will show any problem
choices.feedback: This is exactly backwards. Supplemental oxygen is what delays the oximeter, sometimes by a full minute after breathing has stopped. Oxygen makes capnography more necessary, not less.

choices.text: Delay the sedation for 6 hours because he ate 90 minutes ago
choices.feedback: Emergency sedation is not delayed purely for fasting time, since delay has not been shown to lower aspiration risk here. The intake is documented and it informs drug and depth choice, but a dislocated shoulder is time-sensitive for reduction.

steps.prompt:
The provider says, "I am going to need someone pulling counter-traction with the sheet while I reduce this. You have got a free hand, right?"

What do you say?

choices.text: Take the sheet with one hand and keep watching the monitor with the other
choices.feedback: There is no such thing as monitoring with one hand while pulling counter-traction. The moment your body is committed to the traction you are not watching the patient, and that is exactly when apnea happens.

choices.text: Say that the monitoring role has to stay dedicated, and ask for another person for counter-traction
choices.feedback: Correct, and this is the sentence worth practising. The person watching the patient watches only the patient. Asking for a third set of hands takes ten seconds and is never the wrong call.

choices.text: Agree, but ask the provider to glance at the monitor periodically
choices.feedback: The provider is looking at a shoulder and cannot reliably watch a waveform at the same time. Splitting the monitoring role between two distracted people is not monitoring.

choices.text: Suggest the reduction technique that needs no counter-traction so nobody has to leave their role
choices.feedback: Not your call to make and it sidesteps the real issue, which is staffing. Say plainly that you cannot leave the monitor and ask for help.

steps.prompt:
Propofol is given. About ninety seconds into the reduction attempt you see the capnogram go flat for three consecutive breath cycles. The pulse oximeter reads `98%` on `4 L` by nasal cannula. His chest is not moving.

What do you do?

choices.text: Say out loud that there is no waveform and no chest rise, and perform a chin lift and jaw thrust
choices.feedback: Right on both counts. Announce it so the room knows, and open the airway. Most sedation events are fixed by a jaw thrust and a few seconds of stimulation.

choices.text: Wait for the pulse oximeter to fall before acting, since the saturation is still 98%
choices.feedback: Waiting throws away the entire warning capnography just gave you. With a lung full of oxygen the saturation can stay high for a minute or more after breathing stops, and by then you are behind.

choices.text: Check the sampling line for a disconnection first, then reassess
choices.feedback: Worth a glance, but not before you look at the patient. A chest that is not moving confirms the waveform. Treat the patient, then troubleshoot the equipment.

choices.text: Give flumazenil immediately
choices.feedback: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and does nothing for propofol. There is no reversal agent for propofol, which is why airway support is the entire plan.

steps.prompt:
The jaw thrust restores a waveform within seconds and his chest begins moving again. The shoulder reduces on the next attempt. The provider is pleased and starts talking about the post-reduction film. The patient is snoring lightly.

The procedure is over. What now?

choices.text: Keep him on full monitoring with capnography, keep the airway open, and continue vitals every 5 minutes
choices.feedback: Correct, and the reasoning matters: the painful stimulus that was keeping him aroused has just been removed, so peak drug effect can land now. This is the most commonly under-monitored part of a sedation.

choices.text: Take the monitor off and move him to a hallway bed so the room can be turned over
choices.feedback: This is the single most dangerous move in the case. The period right after the stimulus stops is when respiratory depression shows up, and a hallway bed has nobody watching.

choices.text: Leave the pulse oximeter on but disconnect the capnography since the procedure is finished
choices.feedback: You are removing the monitor that already saved this patient once today, at the moment it is most likely to be needed again.

choices.text: Continue full monitoring and arrange the post-reduction film and repeat neurovascular check at the bedside
choices.feedback: Good. Bringing the imaging and the recheck to a monitored patient rather than moving a sedated patient to the imaging suite is the right sequence.

steps.prompt:
Thirty-five minutes later he is awake, oriented, comfortable in a sling and swathe, vitals at baseline, no nausea, and he has walked to the bathroom and back without dizziness. He is asking to leave and says he will drive himself because his car is in the lot.

What do you do?

choices.text: He meets all the other criteria, so discharge him and advise caution on the drive
choices.feedback: He meets every criterion except the one that cannot be waived. Residual sedative effect outlasts an alert appearance, and driving is the highest-risk thing he could do in the next few hours.

choices.text: Explain that he cannot drive, arrange a responsible adult to take him and observe him, and give written instructions: no driving, machinery, alcohol or legal decisions for 24 hours
choices.feedback: Correct and complete. A responsible adult is a discharge criterion, not a courtesy, and the restrictions run 24 hours rather than until he feels normal.

choices.text: Keep him for another two hours and then let him drive
choices.feedback: An arbitrary extra wait does not substitute for a responsible adult, and it ties up a bed. The rule is not about time in the department, it is about who takes him home and who watches him.

choices.text: Have him sign a form refusing the ride and let him go
choices.feedback: A signature does not make an unsafe discharge safe, and it does not protect him or anyone else on the road. Solve the transport problem instead.

scenarios.debrief:
Three moments decided this case, and none of them was the shoulder. The first was refusing to give up the dedicated monitoring role for a pair of hands on a sheet. The second was acting on a flat capnogram while the pulse oximeter still read 98 percent, because supplemental oxygen buys a patient a minute of falsely reassuring numbers after breathing has already stopped. The third was keeping full monitoring on after the reduction, when the painful stimulus that was holding the patient awake disappeared and peak drug effect could finally show.

The discharge step is the quiet one. Every criterion he met was visible: awake, oriented, stable, walking, comfortable. The criterion he failed was the one that lives outside the room, and no amount of extra observation time substitutes for a responsible adult and written 24-hour restrictions.
